intro: -잖아(요) (-janha-yo) means "you know" or "as you know." You use it to remind someone of something they already know, or should know, usually to explain a reason or back up your point. It comes from -지 않아(요), "isn't it?", squeezed into one short ending.
usage: -잖아(요) points to shared knowledge. The speaker assumes the listener already knows the fact, so it works like "you know," "remember?" or "come on, it's obvious." It often gives the reason for something just said.

The tone can be friendly ("you know how it is") or a little sharp ("I already told you!"), depending on the situation and your voice. Because it reminds the listener of something, it can sound like you are correcting them.

Use 잖아 with friends and people younger than you. Add 요 (잖아요) for polite speech with people you don't know well. With a boss or an older person, be careful: even 잖아요 can sound like "you should know this."

examples.en: I told you!

examples.context: Explaining why the shop is closed
examples.en: It's Sunday today, you know.
You can't eat spicy food, remember?
It's raining outside, you know.

compare.note: -거든요 gives a reason the listener did NOT know yet ("you see"), while -잖아요 points to something the listener already knows ("you know").
-죠 checks or seeks agreement ("right?") and sounds softer. -잖아요 is more insistent, as if the fact is obvious.

mistakes: Using -잖아요 for news the listener has never heard. If they don't know it yet, use -거든요 instead.
Thinking the 요 makes it safe with anyone. 잖아요 to a boss or teacher can sound like you are scolding them, so it is safer to just state the fact politely.

faq.q: What does 잖아 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 잖아 means "you know" or "come on, you know that." It reminds the listener of a fact you both know. 잖아요 is the polite version.

faq.q: Is 잖아요 rude?
faq.a: Not by itself, and people use it all the time. But since it implies "you should already know this," it can sound pushy, especially toward someone older or higher in rank.

faq.q: What is the difference between 잖아요 and 거든요?
faq.a: Use 잖아요 when the listener already knows the fact, and 거든요 when you are telling them something new as an explanation.

intro: -거든(요) (-geodeun-yo) means "you see" or "it's because." You put it at the end of a sentence to give a reason or background the listener didn't know yet. It is very common in everyday conversation.
usage: -거든(요) explains. It usually comes right after something that needs a reason: why you're late, why you can't come, why you're tired. It is like adding "you see" in English.
It is also used to set up a story. You give some background with -거든, and the listener waits for the rest: "So I went to the store yesterday, right? And..."
거든 is casual, for friends and younger people. 거든요 is polite and fine with coworkers or strangers. In very formal speech, like a presentation, people use -기 때문입니다 instead.

examples.en: The traffic was really bad, you see.
I ate a little while ago, you see.
So I watched a movie yesterday, right?
I have an exam tomorrow, you see.

compare.note: -잖아요 reminds the listener of something they already know. -거든요 tells them something new.
-아서/어서 links a reason inside one sentence ("I'm late because..."). -거든요 ends the sentence and adds the reason afterward, like a separate explanation.

mistakes: Using -거든요 for a fact the listener already knows. That situation calls for -잖아요.
Mixing it up with -거든 in the middle of a sentence. 도착하거든 전화해 means "call me when you arrive," which is a different, more bookish "if/when" use.

faq.q: What does 거든요 mean?
faq.a: 거든요 means "you see" or "because." It gives a reason or background the listener didn't know.

faq.q: What is the difference between 거든요 and 잖아요?
faq.a: 거든요 shares new information as an explanation. 잖아요 points to information the listener already knows.

faq.q: Can 거든 mean "if"?
faq.a: Yes, in the middle of a sentence, -거든 can mean "if" or "when," usually followed by a request or suggestion, as in 시간 있거든 와 ("come if you have time"). At the end of a sentence it means "you see."

intro: -더라(고요) (-deora-goyo) means "I noticed that" or "I found that." You use it to tell someone about something you saw, heard or felt yourself in the past. It is like sharing a fresh first-hand report.

formation.when: Past (already done when you saw it)

usage: -더라(고요) reports something you experienced directly: a place you visited, food you tasted, a person you met. The feeling is "here's what I found when I was there."

The subject is usually someone or something else, not you. When the subject is you, it is mostly about feelings or reactions you noticed in yourself, like 저도 좀 무섭더라고요 ("I found I was a bit scared too").
더라 and 더라고 are casual, for friends. 더라고요 is polite and very common in conversation. 더라 can also sound like you're thinking out loud.

examples.en: That restaurant was really good.
It was colder outside than I thought.

examples.context: Telling a friend what you saw
examples.en: Minsu had already gone home.
That movie was kind of sad.

compare.note: -던데요 also shares something you saw yourself, but it leaves the sentence open, often hinting at a contrast or inviting a reaction.
The plain past just states a fact. -더라고요 adds "I saw or felt this myself," so it sounds more vivid and personal.

mistakes: Using it for your own planned actions. "I ate lunch" is 점심을 먹었어요, not 점심을 먹더라고요.
Using it for things you only heard about secondhand. For hearsay, use -대요/-래요.

faq.q: What does 더라고요 mean?
faq.a: It means "I noticed" or "I found that." You use it to report something you saw or experienced yourself in the past.

faq.q: What is the difference between 더라 and 더라고요?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 더라 is casual, 더라고 is casual and chatty, and 더라고요 is the polite version.

faq.q: Can I use 더라고요 about myself?
faq.a: Mostly for your own feelings or reactions, like 생각보다 재미있더라고요 about something you tried. For things you simply did, use the normal past tense.

intro: -구나/-군요 (-guna/-gunyo) means "oh, I see" or "so that's how it is." You use it when you notice or realize something new right now. -구나 is casual and -군요 is polite.
usage: -구나/-군요 shows a small "aha" moment. You have just seen, heard or understood something, and you react to it. In English it is like "Oh, so..." or "I see."
-구나 is casual. People often say it to themselves, or to friends, children and younger people. Parents and older characters in dramas use it a lot when talking to someone younger.
-군요 is polite. It can sound a little formal or thoughtful in speech, so in casual polite talk many people use -네요 instead.

examples.en: Oh, it snowed a lot!
You speak Korean well!
So that's why you were late.
So this is your hometown, Minji.

compare.note: -네요 is a quick, emotional reaction to what you see right now. -군요 feels more like understanding or realizing something, and sounds a bit more formal.
-구나 reacts to something in the moment. -더라고요 reports to someone else what you noticed earlier.

mistakes: Forgetting 는 with action verbs in the present. Say 먹는구나, not 먹구나.
Using it for something you already knew. -구나 is for new realizations.

faq.q: What does 구나 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 구나 means "oh, I see" or "so that's it." It shows you just realized something. It is casual.

faq.q: What is the difference between 군요 and 네요?
faq.a: Both react to something new. 네요 is quicker and more emotional, and very common in daily speech. 군요 sounds more like a thoughtful realization and is a bit more formal.

faq.q: When do I use 는구나 instead of 구나?
faq.a: Use 는구나 with action verbs in the present tense (먹는구나). Use 구나 with adjectives, nouns and the past tense (예쁘구나, 왔구나).

intro: -(으)ㄹ래(요) (-(eu)llae-yo) means "I'll" or "I want to" in a statement, and "do you want to?" in a question. It is about what someone feels like doing. You hear it constantly when friends make plans or order food.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

usage: In a statement, -(으)ㄹ래요 tells your own choice or wish: 저는 커피 마실래요 ("I'll have coffee"). In a question, it asks the other person what they want: 뭐 먹을래? ("What do you want to eat?").
It is only used with verbs, and only about "I" in statements or "you" in questions. For what someone else wants, use -고 싶어 해요.
-(으)ㄹ래 is casual. -(으)ㄹ래요 is polite but still friendly and relaxed. With a boss or in formal service, people use -(으)시겠어요? instead, as in 뭐 드시겠어요?

examples.en: I'll have bibimbap.
Want to watch a movie together?
I don't want to go.
Do you want to sit here?

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise or decision made with the listener in mind ("I'll do it for you"). -(으)ㄹ래요 is simply what you feel like doing.
-(으)ㄹ까요? suggests "shall we?" or asks for an opinion. -(으)ㄹ래요? asks what the listener personally wants.
학생이래요 means "they say he's a student," a shortened quote. The "want to" ending always has ㄹ attached to a verb, as in 갈래요.

mistakes: Using it for a third person. "Minsu wants to go" is 민수는 가고 싶어 해요, not 민수는 갈래요.
Asking a boss 커피 마실래요? It sounds too casual. Try 커피 드시겠어요? instead.

faq.q: What does 래요 mean in 갈래요?
faq.a: In 갈래요, -ㄹ래요 means "I'll" or "I want to." As a question, 갈래요? means "Do you want to go?"

faq.q: What is the difference between 할래요 and 할게요?
faq.a: 할래요 is your own wish ("I want to do it"). 할게요 is a promise or decision, often for the listener's sake ("I'll do it, don't worry").

faq.q: Is 을래요 polite?
faq.a: It is polite but casual in feel. It is great with friends, coworkers and people your age, but less fitting with a boss or customers.

intro: -(으)ㄹ까(요) (-(eu)lkka-yo) means "shall we?", "shall I?" or "I wonder." It turns a sentence into a soft question that asks for the listener's opinion. It is one of the most useful question endings in Korean.
usage: With 우리 (we), it suggests doing something together: 우리 갈까요? ("Shall we go?"). With 제가 (I), it offers to do something: 제가 할까요? ("Shall I do it?").
With other subjects, or with adjectives, it means "I wonder" or "do you think?": 내일 비가 올까요? ("Do you think it will rain tomorrow?").
-(으)ㄹ까 is casual. -(으)ㄹ까요 is polite and soft, so it is a safe way to suggest something even to people above you.

examples.en: Shall we have lunch together?
Shall I open the window?
Will it rain tomorrow, I wonder?
Do you think these clothes are okay?

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ래요? asks what the listener wants. -(으)ㄹ까요? suggests something or asks for their opinion.
-(으)ㅂ시다 directly says "let's." -(으)ㄹ까요 is softer because it asks first.

mistakes: Answering a question with the same ending. If someone asks 제가 할까요?, answer 네, 해 주세요, not 네, 할까요.
Using a consonant stem without 을. Say 먹을까요, not 먹까요.

faq.q: What does 을까요 mean?
faq.a: It means "shall we?", "shall I?" or "do you think?" It makes a soft suggestion or asks for an opinion.

faq.q: How do I answer 갈까요?
faq.a: If it means "shall we go?", answer 네, 가요 or 좋아요. If it means "shall I go?", answer 네, 가세요 or 아니요, 괜찮아요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 할까요 and 할래요?
faq.a: 할까요? is "shall we/I do it?" and asks for your opinion. 할래요? is "do you want to do it?" and asks about your wish.

intro: -자 (-ja) means "let's." It is the casual way to suggest doing something together, used with friends and people younger than you. It attaches straight to any verb stem.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in ㄹ (no change)

usage: -자 makes a simple, direct suggestion: "let's go," "let's eat," "let's do it." It works only with verbs.
It is casual speech (반말). Use it with close friends, siblings, or people younger than you. To be polite, say the -아요/어요 form with a suggesting tone (가요!), or ask with -(으)ㄹ까요?
For "let's not," use -지 말자. Don't use 안 with -자.

examples.en: Let's hang out this weekend.
Let's eat.
Let's go, quick!
Let's not fight today.

compare.note: -(으)ㅂ시다 is the formal "let's," used to groups or in announcements. -자 is for friends and younger people.
갈까? asks "shall we go?" and leaves room for the other person to decide. 가자 is a direct "let's go."

mistakes: Saying 가자 to someone older, like a teacher or boss. Use 가요 or 갈까요? instead.
Saying 안 가자 for "let's not go." The correct form is 가지 말자.

faq.q: What does 자 mean at the end of a Korean verb?
faq.a: It means "let's." 가자 is "let's go" and 먹자 is "let's eat." It is casual.

faq.q: What is the polite way to say 가자?
faq.a: Say 가요 with a suggesting tone, or ask 갈까요? ("shall we go?"). 갑시다 exists too, but it sounds like you're leading a group.

faq.q: How do you say "let's not" in Korean?
faq.a: Use -지 말자, as in 가지 말자 ("let's not go").

intro: -(으)ㅂ시다 (-(eu)psida) means "let's" in a formal way. You hear it in meetings, announcements, signs and speeches. Even though it looks polite, it is not the right way to say "let's" to your boss or an older person.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant
Verb stem ending in ㄹ (ㄹ drops)

usage: -(으)ㅂ시다 suggests doing something together in a clear, formal voice. A team leader might say it to a team, or a public sign might say it to everyone.
It sounds like the speaker is in charge. That's why you shouldn't use it to someone older or higher in rank. For them, use -(으)ㄹ까요? or -(으)시지요.
Among friends, use -자 instead. With coworkers at your level, -아요/어요 (가요!) often sounds more natural.

examples.en: Let's start the meeting.
Let's not litter.
Let's all do our best!
Let's have lunch now.

compare.note: -자 is the casual "let's" for friends. -(으)ㅂ시다 is formal and fits groups and announcements.
-(으)시지요 (often 시죠) is a respectful way to suggest something to someone above you, like 가시죠 ("shall we go?").

mistakes: Saying 갑시다 to your boss to be polite. It can sound like you are giving orders. Try 가시죠 or 갈까요? instead.
Keeping ㄹ in ㄹ verbs. Say 만듭시다, not 만들읍시다.

faq.q: What does 갑시다 mean?
faq.a: 갑시다 means "let's go" in a formal way. It comes from 가다 plus -ㅂ시다.

faq.q: Is 읍시다 polite?
faq.a: It is formal, but it is not respectful toward people above you. It works best when speaking to a group or in announcements.

faq.q: What is the difference between 갑시다 and 가자?
faq.a: 가자 is casual, for friends. 갑시다 is formal, used by someone leading a group or on signs.

intro: -아라/어라 (-ara/-eora) is a casual command, like "do it!" Parents say it to children and older people say it to much younger ones. It is the command form of the plain speech style.
usage: -아라/어라 gives a direct order. It is used by parents to children, teachers to young students, and older people to someone much younger. In dramas you'll hear it in family scenes: 밥 먹어라 ("come eat").
It can sound strong. Between friends, the plain -아/어 form (먹어!) is more common and softer. To anyone you're not close to, use -(으)세요.
With some adjectives, -아라/어라 is not a command but an exclamation, like 아이고 추워라 ("ugh, it's so cold!").

examples.en: Go to bed early.
Eat a lot.
Study hard.
Ugh, it's so cold!

compare.note: 먹어! is the everyday casual command between friends. 먹어라 sounds firmer or more like a parent talking.
-(으)세요 is the polite request, used with anyone you're not close to.
When you quote a command, use (으)라: 먹으라고 했어요 ("they told me to eat"), not 먹어라고.

mistakes: Using it with strangers, coworkers or older people. It sounds bossy or rude. Use -(으)세요 instead.
Quoting a command with 어라. Say 가라고 했어요 and 먹으라고 했어요.

faq.q: What does 해라 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 해라 means "do it!" It is the casual command form of 하다, used by parents or older people to someone younger.

faq.q: Is 아라/어라 rude?
faq.a: It isn't rude between parents and children or to someone much younger. To someone your age or older, it sounds bossy.

faq.q: What is the difference between 먹어 and 먹어라?
faq.a: Both are casual commands. 먹어 is the everyday one among friends. 먹어라 is firmer and sounds more like a parent or older person.

intro: -지 마세요/-지 마 (-ji maseyo/-ji ma) means "don't." You add it to a verb to tell someone not to do something. -지 마세요 is polite and -지 마 is casual.

formation.example: 가다 → 가지 마세요, 먹다 → 먹지 마세요

usage: -지 마세요 comes from 말다 (to stop, not do) and makes a negative command: "don't do it." It attaches to verbs.
Pick the level that fits the person: 지 마 for friends and younger people, 지 마세요 for most polite situations, and 지 마십시오 for formal signs and announcements.
You'll also hear 아프지 마 ("don't get sick") as a caring wish, even though 아프다 is an adjective. For feelings, Korean usually uses the -아/어하다 form: 슬퍼하지 마세요 ("don't be sad").

examples.en: Don't worry.
Don't cry.
Please don't take pictures.
Don't push yourself too hard.

compare.note: 안 가세요 means "you're not going" or "aren't you going?" To tell someone not to go, say 가지 마세요.
-(으)세요 asks someone to do something. -지 마세요 asks them not to.

mistakes: Using 안 for a negative command. "Don't eat" is 먹지 마세요, not 안 먹으세요.
Using it with feeling adjectives. "Don't be sad" is 슬퍼하지 마세요, using the -아/어하다 verb form, rather than 슬프지 마세요.

faq.q: What does 하지 마 mean?
faq.a: 하지 마 means "don't do it." It is casual. The polite version is 하지 마세요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 지 마 and 지 마세요?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 지 마 is for friends and younger people, and 지 마세요 is polite.

faq.q: What does 아프지 마 mean?
faq.a: It means "don't get sick" or "stay well." People say it to show they care.

intro: -ㄴ/는다 (-n/neunda) is the plain form of a verb, like 간다 ("goes") or 먹는다 ("eats"). It is used in writing such as books, diaries, news and essays, and in casual speech to close friends. It has no politeness added, so it is neutral on paper but casual out loud.

formation.when: Action verb, stem ends in a vowel
Action verb, stem ends in a consonant
Action verb, stem ends in ㄹ (ㄹ drops)

usage: This is the style of written Korean. Novels, diaries, newspapers, essays and school reports use it: 나는 매일 학교에 간다 ("I go to school every day").
In speech, it is casual. Friends use it to announce or exclaim something: 나 간다! ("I'm off!") or 비 온다! ("It's raining!"). Never use it with people you need to be polite to.
Only action verbs in the present take ㄴ/는. Adjectives stay in dictionary form (좋다), and the past tense just adds 다 (먹었다).

examples.en: I read a book every morning.
I'm heading out first.
Wow, it's snowing!
Koreans eat tteokguk on Lunar New Year.

compare.note: -아요/어요 is the everyday polite style for speaking. -ㄴ/는다 is for writing, or for talking to close friends.
-(스)ㅂ니다 is formal and polite, used in speeches and news broadcasts. -ㄴ/는다 is neutral in writing but casual when spoken.

mistakes: Adding 는다 to adjectives. Say 좋다, not 좋는다, and 예쁘다, not 예쁜다.
Adding ㄴ/는 to the past tense. Say 갔다, not 갔는다.

faq.q: What is the 는다 form in Korean?
faq.a: It is the plain style of a verb, like 먹는다 ("eats"). It is used in writing and in casual speech between close friends.

faq.q: Why do Korean books and diaries use 는다?
faq.a: Written Korean usually doesn't address a specific listener, so it uses this plain style instead of polite endings like -아요/어요.

faq.q: When do you use ㄴ다 and when 는다?
faq.a: Use ㄴ다 after a verb stem ending in a vowel (간다) and 는다 after a consonant (먹는다). For ㄹ verbs, drop the ㄹ and add ㄴ다 (살다 → 산다).

intro: -냐 (-nya) and -니 (-ni) are casual question endings, the plain way to ask "do you...?" or "is it...?" to a friend, a younger person, or a child. -니 sounds soft and gentle, while -냐 sounds more blunt and rough. Both are banmal (casual speech), so they are never used with people you should be polite to.
usage: Both endings turn a sentence into a casual question. You use them only with people you would speak banmal to: close friends, younger siblings, kids.
-니 has a gentle, caring tone. Parents and teachers often use it with children (밥 먹었니?), and friends use it when they want to sound soft.

-냐 is more direct and can sound rough or challenging, especially with a sharp tone. It is very common between close male friends and in online comments. With the wrong person or tone, it can sound rude.
The most neutral casual question is simply the 아/어 form with rising intonation (먹어?). -니 and -냐 add their own flavor on top of that.

examples.en: Did you eat?
Where are you right now?
Is this really good?

examples.context: Asking a younger cousin about plans
examples.en: What are you doing this weekend?

compare.note: The plain casual question (먹어?) is the most neutral and common. -니 sounds softer and -냐 sounds blunter than it.
These are soft polite questions for strangers or people above you. -냐 and -니 are casual only.

mistakes: Using -냐 or -니 with an older person, a coworker, or a stranger. They are banmal and will sound rude.
Keeping the ㄹ on ㄹ stems: 살다 becomes 사니?, not 살니?.

faq.q: What is the difference between -니 and -냐?
faq.a: Both are casual questions. -니 sounds soft and gentle, like a parent or kind older friend, while -냐 sounds blunt and is common among close friends, especially men.

faq.q: Is -냐 rude?
faq.a: It is not rude between close friends, but it is banmal and can sound rough. Never use it with someone older or someone you just met.

faq.q: What does 뭐 하니 mean?
faq.a: 뭐 하니? means "What are you doing?" in a soft, casual way, often said by an older person to a younger one.

intro: -나요 (-nayo) and -(으)ㄴ가요 (-(eu)ngayo) are polite question endings that sound softer and gentler than the usual -아요/어요?. You use -나요 with verbs and -(으)ㄴ가요 with adjectives and nouns. They are common when asking strangers, staff, or anyone you want to be careful with.
usage: These endings make a question sound gentle and less direct, a bit like "Is it...?" or "Do you happen to...?" in English. They are polite, so you can use them with strangers, shop staff, teachers, and coworkers.
They also work when you are wondering out loud, almost asking yourself: 왜 안 오나요? can mean "Why isn't he coming, I wonder?"
In everyday speech you will also hear -나요 after adjectives, especially 괜찮나요?. It is very common, but -(으)ㄴ가요 is the textbook pattern for adjectives.
The casual versions are -나? and -(으)ㄴ가?, which often sound like you are thinking to yourself.

examples.en: Does this bus go to City Hall?

examples.context: Asking a coworker for a minute
examples.en: Do you have time, by any chance?

examples.context: Checking on someone who is sick
examples.en: Does it hurt a lot?
Is the meeting already over?

compare.note: The standard polite question. -나요 and -(으)ㄴ가요 sound softer and a little more careful.
These are casual questions for friends and younger people, not polite ones.
-나 보다 is not a question. It means "it seems that" based on what you see.

mistakes: Putting -나요 straight onto a noun. Say 학생인가요?, not 학생나요?.
Keeping the ㄹ on ㄹ stems: 알다 becomes 아나요?, not 알나요?.

faq.q: Is -나요 more polite than -아요/어요?
faq.a: It is about the same level of politeness, but it sounds softer and less direct, so it often feels more considerate.

faq.q: When do I use -나요 and when -(으)ㄴ가요?
faq.a: Use -나요 with verbs, 있다/없다, and any past tense. Use -(으)ㄴ가요 with adjectives and 인가요 with nouns.

faq.q: What does 괜찮나요 mean?
faq.a: 괜찮나요? means "Is it okay?" or "Are you okay?" in a soft, polite way.

intro: -는 거야 (-neun geoya) and -는 거예요 (-neun geoyeyo) mean "it's that..." or "the thing is...", and they turn a sentence into an explanation of a situation. In questions they ask for the story behind something, like "So you're going where?" or "Why is it that you're crying?". 거 is the spoken short form of 것 (thing).

formation.example: 가다 → 간 거예요, 먹다 → 먹은 거예요

usage: This pattern frames what you say as an explanation. In a statement it means "it's that..." or "that's how it is": 이렇게 하는 거야 means "This is how you do it."

In questions, often with 왜 or 어디, it asks the other person to explain the situation: 왜 우는 거야? sounds like "Why are you crying? What's going on?" It can sound curious, worried, or annoyed depending on tone.
거야 is casual (banmal), 거예요 is polite, and 것입니다 or 겁니다 is formal. 거야 also appears as a firm statement: 난 갈 거야 is future, but 그냥 가는 거야 means "We're just going, that's that."

examples.en: Where are you going right now?
Why are you crying?
This is how you do it
Did you already eat it all?

compare.note: 갈 거예요 means "I will go" (future). 가는 거예요 means "it's that I'm going", explaining a present situation.
-거든요 gives a reason the listener didn't know. -는 거예요 frames the whole situation as an explanation.

mistakes: Mixing up 가는 거예요 (it's that I'm going) and 갈 거예요 (I will go).
Spelling it 거에요. The correct spelling is 거예요.

faq.q: What does 거야 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 거야 is a casual way to say "it is (the thing)". After a verb, as in 가는 거야, it means "it's that (someone) is going" and explains a situation.

faq.q: What is the difference between 가는 거야 and 갈 거야?
faq.a: 갈 거야 is future: "I'm going to go." 가는 거야 describes or asks about what is happening now: "It's that I'm going" or "Are you going?"

faq.q: Is it 거예요 or 거에요?
faq.a: 거예요 is correct. 거에요 is a very common misspelling.

intro: -(으)ㄹ걸 (-(eu)lgeol) has two meanings: "I should have..." when you regret something, and "probably..." or "I bet..." when you make a guess. Regret is usually said to yourself with a falling tone, while the guess is often said as -(으)ㄹ걸요 with a lifting tone at the end.
usage: Regret: attached to a verb, it means "I should have done that" (and didn't). It is like a sigh to yourself, so it normally has no 요: 우산 가져올걸. To say it politely to someone, Koreans add 그랬어요: 가져올 걸 그랬어요.

Guess: with verbs, adjectives, nouns, or past tense, it means "probably" or "I think". Add 요 to be polite: 지금쯤 도착했을걸요. This guess often gently goes against what the other person expects, like "Actually, I think...".
Your tone tells people which meaning you want. A falling, sighing tone sounds like regret. A light tone that rises a little at the end sounds like a guess.

examples.en: I should have gone to bed earlier
I should have just stayed home
They've probably arrived by now
Minsu probably doesn't know

compare.note: This also means "I should have", but it is stronger and more serious. -(으)ㄹ걸 is a lighter sigh of regret.
Both can guess, but -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is neutral. -(으)ㄹ걸요 sounds more like "I bet" and can hint you disagree.
-(으)ㄹ 텐데 is a guess that leads into something else, like advice or worry. -(으)ㄹ걸 ends the thought.

mistakes: Adding 요 to a regret: 살걸요 sounds like a guess ("probably"), not a regret. For polite regret, say 살 걸 그랬어요.

faq.q: What does 할걸 mean?
faq.a: It can mean "I should have done it" (regret) or "they'll probably do it" (guess). The context and tone tell you which one.

faq.q: What is the difference between -(으)ㄹ걸 and -았/었어야 했는데?
faq.a: Both express regret, but -(으)ㄹ걸 is light and casual, like a sigh. -았/었어야 했는데 sounds heavier and more serious.

intro: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 (-(eu)l tende) means "it would probably be..." or "I bet...", and it sets up what comes next, like advice, a worry, or a wish. For example, 피곤할 텐데 쉬어 means "You must be tired, so rest." At the end of a sentence, -(으)ㄹ 텐데(요) leaves a feeling of worry or wishing hanging in the air.
usage: The first part is your guess about a situation, and the second part reacts to it: advice, a suggestion, or a worry. 비가 올 텐데 우산 가져가 means "It'll probably rain, so take an umbrella."
With 좋다 it often expresses a wish: 같이 가면 좋을 텐데 means "It would be nice if we could go together" (but we probably can't). With past tense, 좋았을 텐데 means "it would have been nice".
Ending a sentence with -(으)ㄹ 텐데 or -(으)ㄹ 텐데요 sounds caring or worried, like "I'm worried that...". Use 요 with people you speak politely to.

examples.context: Seeing a friend after a long shift
examples.en: You must be really tired, so rest a bit
If we go now, we'll probably be late
It would be nice if we went together

examples.context: Wondering why no one has called
examples.en: They must have arrived already

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 테니까 gives a reason ("since it will..." or "since I will..."), often for a request. -(으)ㄹ 텐데 adds a feeling of worry, contrast, or wishing.
-(으)ㄹ걸 makes a guess and stops there. -(으)ㄹ 텐데 usually leads into advice or a feeling.

mistakes: Writing it without a space, like 올텐데. The standard spelling puts a space before 텐데: 올 텐데.

faq.q: What does 텐데 mean?
faq.a: 텐데 comes from 터인데 and means roughly "it would probably be, so/but". It shows a guess and links it to advice, worry, or a wish.

faq.q: Is it 할텐데 or 할 텐데?
faq.a: The standard spelling is 할 텐데, with a space. You will often see 할텐데 online, but it is not the official spelling.

faq.q: What is the difference between 텐데 and 테니까?
faq.a: 테니까 gives a clear reason, often before a request. 텐데 is softer and carries worry, contrast, or a wish.

intro: -던데(요) (-deonde(yo)) means "I noticed that..." or "from what I saw...", and it shares something you saw or experienced yourself, usually setting up a follow-up or a gentle contrast. It is like -더라 (I noticed) combined with -는데 (background, but).
usage: -던데 reports something you personally noticed in the past, then leaves room for more: advice, a question, or a contrast. 그 카페 조용하던데 means "That cafe was quiet (I noticed), so..."
As a sentence ending, -던데요 often gently disagrees or adds your own experience: if someone says a restaurant is bad, you can reply 맛있던데요 ("Hmm, I thought it was good").
It is normally about things you observed, not your own actions. For your own feelings or reactions it works fine: 난 재미있던데 means "I found it fun, though."
-던데 is casual and -던데요 is polite.

examples.en: That restaurant was pretty good, actually
It was really cold outside

examples.context: Someone is looking for a coworker
examples.en: Minji left work a while ago
That cafe was quiet, want to study there?

compare.note: -더라고요 simply reports what you noticed. -던데요 does the same but leaves something unsaid, like a contrast or a follow-up.
-는데 gives background about now. -던데 gives background based on what you saw or felt before.

mistakes: Using -던데 for your own actions, like 내가 밥을 먹던데. It is for things you observed, so it sounds strange about yourself.

faq.q: What does 던데요 mean?
faq.a: It means "I noticed that..." or "from what I saw...", often with a soft "but" or "so" left at the end. It is polite.

faq.q: What is the difference between -던데 and -는데?
faq.a: -는데 talks about the present situation. -던데 recalls something you personally saw or experienced before.

intro: -대요 (-daeyo) and -래요 (-raeyo) mean "they say..." or "I heard...", and they pass on what someone else said. They are short spoken forms of -다고 해요 and -(이)라고 해요. -래요 can also pass on a command, like "she told me to...".
usage: Use -대요 and -래요 to pass on information you heard from someone else, the news, or a forecast. 내일 비 온대요 means "They say it'll rain tomorrow."
-래요 has two jobs: after a noun it means "they say it's (noun)", and after a verb stem it means "they told (me/us) to". 오래요 means "She told us to come."
The casual forms drop 요: 간대, 의사래. As a question, 간대요? means "Did they say they're going?"
Similar short forms exist for other reported speech: -재요 for suggestions ("they said let's") and -냬요 for questions ("they asked if").

examples.en: They say it'll rain tomorrow

examples.context: Passing on news about a friend
examples.en: Minsu says he's moving
I heard that person is a doctor
The teacher told us to come early tomorrow

compare.note: -데요 (with ㅔ) means "I noticed" from your own experience, like -더라고요. -대요 (with ㅐ) means someone else said it.
This is the full form of -대요. It sounds a bit more formal or careful; -대요 is what people usually say.

mistakes: Mixing up 대요 and 데요. 대요 means "they say"; 데요 means "I noticed myself".
Forgetting 는 with action verbs: say 먹는대요, not 먹대요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 대요 and 데요?
faq.a: 대요 reports what someone else said ("they say"). 데요 reports what you noticed yourself ("I saw that").

faq.q: What does 래요 mean?
faq.a: After a noun, 래요 means "they say it's..." (의사래요, "I heard he's a doctor"). After a verb, it means "they told me to..." (오래요, "they told me to come").

faq.q: Is -대요 polite?
faq.a: Yes, with 요 it is polite. The casual form is -대 or -래.

intro: -다니 (-dani) means "I can't believe that..." and shows surprise, shock, or disbelief about something you just saw or heard. For example, 벌써 11월이라니! means "I can't believe it's already November!" With nouns it becomes -(이)라니.
usage: -다니 reacts to news or a situation with strong surprise. It can be happy ("I can't believe we won!"), shocked, or annoyed, depending on the situation and your tone.
It often ends the sentence on its own with an exclamation mark, or comes before words like 믿을 수 없어 (I can't believe it) or 말도 안 돼 (no way).
Add 요 to sound polite: 그만두다니요? repeats what someone just told you, meaning "You're quitting?!". This is a common way to react with surprise or disagreement.

examples.en: I can't believe it's already November!

examples.context: Seeing a friend in the kitchen
examples.en: I can't believe you're cooking!
I can't believe our team won!
You're quitting? Why?

compare.note: -네요 shows mild surprise or a fresh discovery. -다니 is much stronger, closer to shock or disbelief.
-다고요? asks someone to confirm what they said. -다니요? also repeats it, but with more shock or protest.

mistakes: Using -다니 for small, everyday news. It expresses strong surprise, so it can sound dramatic.
Putting 다니 straight onto a noun. Use (이)라니: 학생이라니, not 학생다니.

faq.q: What does 다니 mean in Korean?
faq.a: At the end of a sentence, -다니 means "I can't believe that..." and shows strong surprise. With nouns it is -(이)라니.

faq.q: Is -다니 polite?
faq.a: On its own it is casual. Add 요 (-다니요) when you are speaking politely.

intro: -지 그래(요) (-ji geurae(yo)) means "why don't you...?" and gives someone a casual suggestion or piece of advice. In the past form, -지 그랬어(요), it means "you should have...", often with a light note of blame.

formation.example: 쉬다 → 쉬지 그래요, 먹다 → 먹지 그래요

usage: Use -지 그래 to suggest something to the person you are talking to: "Why don't you just...?" It sounds natural and friendly with friends and people around your age.
Be careful with tone. Said warmly, it is caring advice. Said sharply, it can sound like "Why didn't you just do that?" and feel a little critical.
-지 그랬어(요) looks back at something already done: 미리 말하지 그랬어 means "You should have told me earlier." It often comes with mild complaint.
With people above you, softer forms like -(으)시는 게 어때요? (how about...) are safer.

examples.en: If you're tired, why don't you rest a bit?

examples.context: A coworker worried about her mom
examples.en: Why don't you call your mom first?

examples.context: Finding out about a problem late
examples.en: You should have told me sooner

examples.context: Seeing someone in a thin jacket
examples.en: Why don't you dress warmly?

compare.note: "How about...?" This is softer and safer with people above you. -지 그래요 sounds more casual and direct.
"Try doing..." This is a polite, gentle suggestion. -지 그래요 sounds more like friendly pushing.

mistakes: Mixing up 그래요 and 그랬어요. 그래요 suggests something now; 그랬어요 says it is too late ("you should have").
Using it with your boss or an elder. It can sound like you are giving them orders.

faq.q: What does 하지 그래 mean?
faq.a: 하지 그래? means "Why don't you do it?" It is a casual suggestion to a friend.

faq.q: What does -지 그랬어 mean?
faq.a: It means "you should have..." about something in the past, often with a little complaint, like 말하지 그랬어 (you should have told me).

intro: -아야지/-어야지 (-ayaji/-eoyaji) means "I should..." or "you should...". Said about yourself, it sounds like a small decision ("I'm going to..."), and said to someone else, it means "you've got to...". It is a short form of -아/어야 하지, and the polite version is -아야죠/-어야죠.
usage: About yourself, -아야지 sounds like you are making up your mind: 오늘은 일찍 자야지 means "I'm going to bed early tonight" or "I should go to bed early tonight." People often say it to themselves.
To someone else, it means "you should" or "of course you have to": 밥은 먹어야지 means "You've got to eat." It can sound caring or a little bossy, depending on tone.
The casual form is -아야지/-어야지. The polite form is -아야죠/-어야죠, which also often means "Of course, it has to be that way."

examples.en: I should go to bed early tonight
You've got to eat
You have to keep your promises
I'm going to start working out tomorrow

compare.note: "Have to" in a neutral, factual way. -아야지 sounds more personal: a resolution, or a firm "you should".
-(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise to the listener. -아야지 is more like telling yourself what you will do.

mistakes: Telling an older person or your boss what they should do with -아야죠. It can sound like you are lecturing them.

faq.q: What does 해야지 mean?
faq.a: 해야지 means "I should do it" or "you should do it". About yourself it sounds like a decision; to someone else it sounds like advice.

faq.q: What is the difference between 해야지 and 해야 돼?
faq.a: 해야 돼 states an obligation ("I have to"). 해야지 sounds more like a resolution or a firm piece of advice.

intro: -겠- (-get-) means "will" when you state your intention, and "must be" or "looks like" when you make a guess from what you see. For example, 제가 하겠습니다 means "I will do it", and 맛있겠다 means "That looks delicious." It goes inside the verb, before endings like -어요 or -습니다.
usage: Intention: about yourself, -겠- means "I will" and sounds firm and polite. It is common in formal settings: 열심히 하겠습니다 (I will work hard). When you ask someone else, it asks what they would like: 뭐 드시겠어요? (What would you like to have?).
Guess: about something you see or hear, it means "must be" or "looks like": 맛있겠다! (That looks tasty!), 힘들었겠어요 (That must have been hard). It is a natural way to show sympathy.
It also appears in set phrases where it makes speech softer and more polite: 알겠습니다 (Understood), 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure), 처음 뵙겠습니다 (Nice to meet you).

examples.en: This looks really delicious
I will do it

examples.context: Hearing about a friend's hard week
examples.en: That must have been really hard
What would you like to have?

compare.note: Both can mean "will" or "probably". -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is more everyday and neutral; -겠- sounds firmer for plans and more on-the-spot for guesses.
-(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise made to the listener ("I'll do it for you"). -겠- is a more formal statement of intention.

mistakes: Using -겠- for another person's plans. 민수가 가겠어요 sounds like a guess ("Minsu will probably go"), not his plan. For other people's plans, use -(으)ㄹ 거예요.

faq.q: What does 겠 mean in Korean?
faq.a: -겠- shows either your intention ("I will") or a guess ("it must be"). Which one depends on whether you are talking about your own action or something you are judging.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 알겠습니다?
faq.a: 알겠습니다 means "Understood" or "Got it". The -겠- makes it sound polite and humble, so it is common at work and with customers.

faq.q: What does 맛있겠다 mean?
faq.a: 맛있겠다 means "That looks delicious" or "That must be tasty". It is a guess based on what you see or smell.

intro: -기 때문에 (-gi ttaemune) means "because" and gives the reason for what comes next. It is a clear, slightly formal way to explain why, and you will see it a lot in writing, news and presentations.

formation.example: 가다 → 가기 때문에, 좋다 → 좋기 때문에
먹다 → 먹었기 때문에, 하다 → 했기 때문에

usage: Put the reason before -기 때문에 and the result after it: "A-기 때문에 B" means "B because A". To give the reason at the end of a sentence, say -기 때문이에요 ("it's because...").

It sounds clear and a little formal, so it fits writing, speeches and careful explanations. In everyday chat, Koreans more often use -아서/어서 or -(으)니까, but -기 때문에 is still fine in speech when you want to stress the reason.
Unlike -아서/어서, you can put past tense on it: 늦었기 때문에 (because I was late).
Do not follow it with a request or suggestion like -(으)세요 or -(으)ㅂ시다. For "It's raining, so take an umbrella", use -(으)니까 instead.

examples.en: I'm tired because I couldn't sleep last night
You can't enter because of construction work
He's popular because he has a good personality
I don't eat out much because prices are high

compare.note: Also means "because", but it is more casual and conversational, and it cannot take past tense (늦었어서 is wrong, 늦어서 is right).
Also gives a reason, but it can be followed by requests and suggestions (비가 오니까 우산 가져가세요), which -기 때문에 cannot.
Right after a noun, 때문에 means "because of" that thing: 비 때문에 (because of the rain). With 이기 때문에 it means "because it is" that noun.

mistakes: Using it before a request: 비가 오기 때문에 우산을 가져가세요 sounds unnatural. Say 비가 오니까 우산을 가져가세요.
Mixing up 학생 때문에 (because of the student) with 학생이기 때문에 (because I am a student).

faq.q: What is the difference between -기 때문에 and -아서/어서?
faq.a: Both mean "because". -기 때문에 sounds firmer and more formal and can take past tense (했기 때문에), while -아서/어서 is the everyday spoken choice and never takes past tense.

faq.q: Can I use -기 때문에 with past tense?
faq.a: Yes. Add 았/었 before 기: 비가 왔기 때문에 (because it rained).

faq.q: What does 때문에 mean on its own?
faq.a: After a noun it means "because of": 너 때문에 (because of you), 일 때문에 (because of work).

intro: -느라(고) (-neura(go)) means "because I was busy doing" something. You use it to explain that one activity took up your time or energy, so something else didn't happen or turned out badly.
usage: -느라(고) links an activity to its usually negative result: "I was busy doing A, so I couldn't do B" or "so I'm tired". It is very common in excuses and apologies.
The person doing both parts is the same, and the first part has to be an activity that takes some time. It works only with verbs, never with adjectives.
Never put past tense on -느라(고) itself. The tense goes on the last verb: 보느라고 못 했어요 (I couldn't do it because I was watching).
고 is often dropped in speech, so 느라 and 느라고 mean the same thing. You can use it in casual or polite speech; the ending of the sentence sets the politeness.

examples.en: I couldn't do my homework because I was playing games
I stayed up all night watching a drama
Sorry, I missed your call because I was hanging out with friends
I was so busy getting ready that my head was spinning

compare.note: Gives an unexpected cause, often something that just happened (an alarm not going off). -느라(고) gives your own time-consuming activity.
A general "because" that works with any verb or adjective. -느라(고) adds the feeling of "I was tied up doing this".

mistakes: Putting past tense on it: 봤느라고 is wrong. Say 보느라고 and put the past tense at the end.
Using it with an adjective or with two different people: 날씨가 춥느라고 is wrong. Use 추워서.

faq.q: Is 느라 the same as 느라고?
faq.a: Yes. 고 is often left out in speech, and the meaning does not change.

faq.q: Can -느라고 be used for good results?
faq.a: It is mostly used for negative or tiring results, like not being able to do something. For a good result, -아서/어서 or 덕분에 sounds more natural.

intro: -는 바람에 (-neun barame) means "because" something unexpected happened, usually leading to a bad result. Think of it as "because suddenly..." or "what with...".

formation.example: 오다 → 오는 바람에, 놓치다 → 놓치는 바람에
잃다 → 잃는 바람에, 늦다 → 늦는 바람에

usage: Use -는 바람에 when something you didn't plan or expect caused a result, usually an inconvenient one: missing the bus, the phone dying, sudden rain.
It always stays -는 바람에, even for past events. The tense goes on the last verb, which is almost always past: 늦잠을 자는 바람에 지각했어요.
It only works with verbs, and it cannot be followed by requests or suggestions. It suits telling what happened, like explaining why you were late.

examples.en: I was late because I missed the bus
I overslept because my alarm didn't go off
I couldn't contact you because my phone died
My clothes got all wet because it suddenly rained

compare.note: Explains that your own time-consuming activity got in the way. -는 바람에 points to an unexpected event, which can be something that happened to you.
A neutral, general "because". -는 바람에 adds the feeling that the cause was sudden or unplanned.
Used when the cause led to a good result (thanks to). -는 바람에 is usually used for bad or inconvenient results.

mistakes: Changing it to past: 온 바람에 or 왔는 바람에 is wrong. It is always 오는 바람에.

faq.q: Why is it -는 바람에 even for past events?
faq.a: That is simply the fixed form. Show the past with the final verb instead: 버스를 놓치는 바람에 늦었어요.

faq.q: Can -는 바람에 be used for good results?
faq.a: Occasionally, but it usually describes something inconvenient. For a good result, -(으)ㄴ 덕분에 (thanks to) is the natural choice.

intro: -더니 (-deoni) links something you saw or experienced in the past to what came after it, like "and then" or "but now". It is used when you are reporting what you noticed, often a change, a contrast or a result.

formation.when: Past (my own action, then what I found)

usage: Plain -더니 describes something you watched happen, usually to someone else or to the weather, and then what followed: a change ("it was cold, but now it's warm"), the next thing they did, or a result ("she practiced hard, and she won").
Because it is based on what you observed, plain -더니 is not usually used for your own actions. For yourself, use -았/었더니: "I did A, and I found B". 약을 먹었더니 나았어요 (I took the medicine and got better).
The second part tells what happened or what you discovered, so it is not followed by commands or suggestions. You can use it in casual or polite speech; the final ending sets the politeness.

examples.en: It was cold this morning, but now it's warm
My little brother came home and went right to sleep
She practiced hard and in the end she won
I took the medicine, and I feel a bit better

compare.note: Means you stopped or switched in the middle of doing something, and the person is the same. -더니 reports a change or result you noticed afterward.
Ends a sentence to share something you noticed. -더니 does the same kind of noticing but links it to what came next.

mistakes: Using plain -더니 for your own action: 제가 공부하더니 합격했어요 sounds odd. Say 제가 열심히 공부했더니 합격했어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between -더니 and -았/었더니?
faq.a: -더니 usually describes what someone else did or how something was, as you saw it. -았/었더니 usually describes your own action and what you found after doing it.

faq.q: Does -더니 always show a contrast?
faq.a: No. It can show a contrast (cold then warm), a next action (came home then slept), or a result (practiced then won).

intro: -다가 (-daga) means "while doing (something), then" and shows that one action was interrupted or switched to another. It is how you say things like "I fell asleep while studying" or "I ran into a friend on my way home".
usage: A-다가 B means you were in the middle of A, then B happened or you switched to B. The same person does both parts.
It often explains how something (usually bad) happened in the middle of an activity: 뛰다가 넘어졌어요 (I fell while running).
With past tense, -았/었다가 means you fully did A and then did something different, often the opposite: 샀다가 환불했어요 (I bought it, then returned it).
In casual speech 가 is often dropped: 가다 친구를 만났어. The politeness comes from the final ending.

examples.en: I fell asleep while studying
I ran into a friend on my way home
I fell while running
I bought the clothes, then got a refund

compare.note: Simply lists actions in order. -다가 shows the first action was interrupted or switched in the middle.
Means "on the way" and is used only with movement verbs. -다가 works with almost any action.
Reports a change or result you observed, often in someone else. -다가 is about the same person switching actions.

mistakes: Using two different people: 엄마가 요리하다가 내가 먹었어요 is wrong. -다가 needs the same person in both parts.

faq.q: What is the difference between -다가 and -고?
faq.a: -고 just means "and then" after finishing. -다가 means you were in the middle of something when you stopped or something else happened.

faq.q: What does -았/었다가 mean?
faq.a: It means you completed an action and then did something different or opposite, like opening a window and then closing it again: 창문을 열었다가 닫았어요.

intro: -는 동안 (-neun dongan) means "while" or "during" and describes a stretch of time in which something else happens. After a noun, 동안 alone means "during" or "for" a period.

formation.example: 자다 → 자는 동안, 먹다 → 먹는 동안

usage: A-는 동안 B means B happens during the time A is going on. The two parts can have different people: 아기가 자는 동안 청소했어요 (I cleaned while the baby slept).
Use 는 even when talking about the past. The tense goes on the final verb.
After a noun or an amount of time, 동안 means "during" or "for": 방학 동안 (during vacation), 두 시간 동안 (for two hours). Adding 에 (동안에) is optional and changes little.

examples.en: Rest while I cook
I cleaned while the baby was sleeping
I learned a lot while living in Korea
What did you do during vacation?

compare.note: Shows one action being interrupted by another, with the same person. -는 동안 just marks a span of time, and the people can differ.
Means doing two things at the same time yourself (eating while watching TV). -는 동안 focuses on the time period.

mistakes: Using past tense before 동안: 잤는 동안 is wrong. Say 자는 동안 and put the past at the end.

faq.q: Is there a difference between 동안 and 동안에?
faq.a: Very little. 에 is optional and often dropped in speech.

faq.q: How do I say "for two hours" in Korean?
faq.a: Put 동안 after the length of time: 두 시간 동안.

intro: -기 전에 (-gi jeone) means "before" doing something. Attach it to a verb to say what happens before that action, like "before eating" or "before bed".
usage: A-기 전에 B means B happens before A. The stem never changes, so it is one of the easiest patterns to use.
Do not put past tense on the verb before 기. Even for past events, keep it plain and put the past tense at the end: 오기 전에 배웠어요.
After a noun, 전에 means "before": 수업 전에 (before class). After a length of time it means "ago": 3년 전에 (three years ago). It works in casual and polite speech alike.

examples.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed
Wash your hands before eating
I'll message you before I leave
I learned Korean before coming to Korea

compare.note: The opposite: "after". Note the different shapes: 먹기 전에 (before eating) but 먹은 후에 (after eating).
Means "until (before)": 끝나기 전까지 기다려요 (I'll wait until it ends).

mistakes: Adding past tense: 먹었기 전에 is wrong. Always say 먹기 전에.

faq.q: How do you say "ago" in Korean?
faq.a: Put 전에 after a length of time: 일주일 전에 (a week ago).

faq.q: Can I use -기 전에 with past tense?
faq.a: Not on the verb before 기. Keep it plain and show the past at the end of the sentence.

intro: -(으)ㄴ 후에 (-(eu)n hue) and -(으)ㄴ 다음에 (-(eu)n daeume) both mean "after" doing something. They tell you that one action happens once another is done.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
formation.example: 보다 → 본 후에, 끝나다 → 끝난 다음에

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a consonant

usage: A-(으)ㄴ 후에 B means B happens after A. The -(으)ㄴ shape is the past modifier, which makes sense because A is already done.
후에 sounds a little more formal or written, while 다음에 is more conversational. 뒤에 is another option with the same meaning.
Even when you talk about the future, the -(으)ㄴ shape stays the same: 먹은 후에 갈게요 (I'll go after I eat). The final ending sets the tense and politeness.

examples.en: I take a walk after eating
Let's meet after class ends
After graduating, I joined a company
I'll call you after I shower

compare.note: Also means "after", with a little more focus on finishing the first action. In most everyday sentences they can swap.
The opposite, "before". It uses a different shape: 먹기 전에 vs 먹은 후에.

mistakes: Using the present modifier: 먹는 후에 is wrong. It is always the past-looking shape 먹은 후에.

faq.q: What is the difference between 후에 and 다음에?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 후에 sounds slightly more formal, and 다음에 is more common in casual conversation.

faq.q: Why is it 먹은 후에 and not 먹는 후에?
faq.a: The first action is finished before the second, so Korean uses the past modifier -(으)ㄴ, even for future plans.

intro: -고 나서 (-go naseo) means "after finishing" something. It stresses that the first action is completely done before the next one starts.
usage: A-고 나서 B means "after finishing A, B". It is close to -(으)ㄴ 후에, but it puts a bit more focus on completing the first action.
The verb before 고 never changes and never takes past tense. Use it with action verbs, not adjectives.
With verbs like 만나다, 가다 or 앉다, where the second action happens in that place or with that person, Koreans usually use -아서/어서 instead: 친구를 만나서 영화를 봤어요 (I met a friend and we watched a movie).

examples.en: Play games after you finish your homework
Take the medicine after eating
I cried after watching the movie
I'll rest after I finish this

compare.note: Means "after" and is usually interchangeable. -고 나서 is a little more conversational and stresses finishing.
Just means "and (then)". -고 나서 makes it clear that the first action was finished first.
Used when the second action depends on the first, like going somewhere and doing something there.

mistakes: Saying 친구를 만나고 나서 영화를 봤어요 to mean you watched the movie with that friend. That sounds like you watched it after you parted. Say 친구를 만나서 영화를 봤어요.
Adding past tense: 먹었고 나서 is wrong. Say 먹고 나서.

faq.q: What is the difference between -고 나서 and -고?
faq.a: -고 simply joins actions. -고 나서 makes it clear the first action was fully finished before the next.

faq.q: Is -고 나서 the same as -(으)ㄴ 후에?
faq.a: Very close, and they are often interchangeable. -고 나서 stresses finishing and sounds a bit more spoken.

intro: -(으)ㄹ 때 (-(eu)l ttae) means "when" and marks the time something happens, like "when I'm bored" or "when I was young". It works with both verbs and adjectives.

formation.example: 가다 → 갈 때, 바쁘다 → 바쁠 때
먹다 → 먹을 때, 덥다 → 더울 때
놀다 → 놀 때, 길다 → 길 때
가다 → 갔을 때, 만나다 → 만났을 때
방학 → 방학 때, 시험 → 시험 때

usage: A-(으)ㄹ 때 B means B happens at the time of A. The -(으)ㄹ shape does not mean future here; it just marks the time.
-았/었을 때 is for a finished event: 한국에 갔을 때 (when I went to Korea, once I was there). 한국에 갈 때 can mean while going or around the time of going.
After certain nouns you can use 때 directly: 방학 때, 시험 때, 어릴 때. Not every time word takes it, though. Days and clock times use 에: 월요일에, not 월요일 때.

examples.en: What do you do when you're bored?
I lived in Busan when I was little
Don't look at your phone while eating
Do you remember when we first met?

compare.note: Means "if" or "whenever" and sets a condition. -(으)ㄹ 때 marks the time something happens.
Stresses a whole stretch of time (while). -(으)ㄹ 때 points to the moment or period more generally.

mistakes: Adding 때 to every time word: 월요일 때 or 세 시 때 is wrong. Use 월요일에, 세 시에.

faq.q: What is the difference between 갈 때 and 갔을 때?
faq.a: 갈 때 is the time of going, often on the way. 갔을 때 is after arriving or once the going had happened: 한국에 갔을 때 친구를 만났어요 (when I went to Korea, I met a friend there).

faq.q: How do you say "when I was young" in Korean?
faq.a: 어릴 때 or 어렸을 때. Both are very common.

intro: -자마자 (-jamaja) means "as soon as" and shows that one thing happens right after another. Attach it to a verb stem with no other changes.
usage: A-자마자 B means B happens immediately after A. The stem never changes, and it is used with verbs only.
No past tense goes on the first verb; the tense goes at the end. The two parts can have different people: 수업이 끝나자마자 비가 왔어요.
It works for past events, future plans and requests: 도착하자마자 전화해 (call me as soon as you arrive). The final ending sets the politeness.

examples.en: I went to sleep as soon as I got home
Call me as soon as you arrive
As soon as class ended, it started to rain
I cried as soon as I heard that song

compare.note: Also "as soon as", but mostly used for future plans and promises (도착하는 대로 연락할게요). -자마자 is common for both past and future.
Just "after finishing", with no sense of speed. -자마자 means right away.

mistakes: Adding past tense: 왔자마자 is wrong. Say 오자마자.

faq.q: What is the difference between -자마자 and -는 대로?
faq.a: Both mean "as soon as". -자마자 is used for past and future, while -는 대로 is mostly for future plans, promises and requests.

faq.q: Can -자마자 be used with adjectives?
faq.a: No, only with verbs.

intro: -는 길에 (-neun gire) means "on the way" to or from somewhere. It is used to say you did something while you were going somewhere, like stopping by a store on the way home.

formation.example: 가다 → 가는 길에, 오다 → 오는 길에
나가다 → 나가는 길에, 퇴근하다 → 퇴근하는 길에

usage: -는 길에 only works with verbs of moving, like 가다, 오다, 나가다, 들어가다, 출근하다 and 퇴근하다. With other actions, use -다가.
길 means "road" or "way", so the pattern literally means "on the road of going". Use 는 even for past trips; the tense goes at the end.
-는 길이에요 (polite) or -는 길이야 (casual) means "I'm on my way": 지금 가는 길이야 (I'm on my way now).

examples.en: I bought bread on my way home
I stopped by the supermarket on my way home from work
I'm on my way to school now
Could you take out the trash on your way out?

compare.note: Works with almost any action and shows an interruption. -는 길에 is only for movement, meaning "on the way".
Means "while I'm at it", using the chance of one action to do another. -는 길에 is specifically about being en route.

mistakes: Using it with non-movement verbs: 공부하는 길에 is wrong. Say 공부하다가.

faq.q: How do you say "I'm on my way" in Korean?
faq.a: 가는 길이에요 (polite) or 가는 길이야 (casual). If you are coming toward the listener, say 가는 길이에요 as well, since Koreans use 가다 for going to where the listener is.

faq.q: What does 길 mean here?
faq.a: 길 means "road" or "way", so -는 길에 is literally "on the way of going".

intro: -도록 (-dorok) means "so that" or "to the point that / until". It shows the goal of an action, or how far an action goes, and -도록 하다 is a polite way to say "make sure to".
usage: "So that": A-도록 B means you do B so that A happens. Unlike -(으)려고, the goal can be about someone else or a situation: 잘 보이도록 크게 써 주세요 (write big so it can be seen).
"Until / to the point that": it shows how long or how far something went, as in 밤새도록 (all night long) or 목이 아프도록 (until my throat hurt).
-도록 하세요 is a polite, slightly formal instruction you hear from teachers, doctors and announcements. -도록 하겠습니다 means "I'll make sure to" and sounds very polite, like at work.

examples.en: Be careful not to catch a cold
Please write big so people in the back can see

examples.context: A long night with a friend
examples.en: We talked all night long
I'll make sure to finish it by tomorrow

compare.note: Means "in order to" for the subject's own intention (I study to pass). -도록 can be about someone else or a situation, and it sounds more formal.
Can also mean "so that" (잘 보이게) and is more casual. -도록 sounds a bit more formal or written.

mistakes: Translating -도록 하세요 as "make someone do". It is a polite instruction meaning "please make sure to".

faq.q: What does -도록 하세요 mean?
faq.a: It is a polite instruction, like "please make sure to": 늦지 않도록 하세요 (please make sure not to be late).

faq.q: What is the difference between -도록 and -게?
faq.a: Both can mean "so that". -게 is more casual and common in speech, while -도록 sounds more formal and also has the "until" meaning (밤새도록).

intro: -(으)ㄹ수록 (-(eu)lsurok) means "the more ... the more". It says that as the first thing increases, the second thing changes along with it. It is often doubled up with -(으)면, as in 보면 볼수록 ("the more I look").
usage: Use -(으)ㄹ수록 when one thing grows or continues and another thing grows or changes with it: the more you practice, the easier it gets. It works with both verbs and adjectives.
The doubled form -(으)면 -(으)ㄹ수록 (보면 볼수록, 들으면 들을수록) adds emphasis and is very common in everyday speech. The second half often has 더 (more) or -아/어지다 (become).
The pattern itself has no politeness level. How polite the sentence is depends on the ending at the very end, like 좋아요 (polite) or 좋아 (casual).

examples.en: The more I see her, the prettier she looks.
The more I eat, the hungrier I get.

examples.context: Getting used to a new city
examples.en: As time goes by, it keeps getting better.
The sooner, the better.

compare.note: -(으)면서 means two things happen at the same time (eating while watching TV). -(으)ㄹ수록 means one thing increases as the other does.
점점 is an adverb meaning "gradually, more and more" on its own. -(으)ㄹ수록 links two clauses and says what the change depends on.

mistakes: With ㄹ-stems, do not add another 을: 만들다 becomes 만들수록, not 만들을수록.
수록 is attached to the verb with no space: write 갈수록, not 갈 수록.

faq.q: What does 갈수록 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 갈수록 comes from 가다 (to go) + -ㄹ수록, so it literally means "the more it goes." In practice it means "as time goes on" or "increasingly," as in 갈수록 추워져요 (It's getting colder and colder).

faq.q: Do I need -(으)면 before -(으)ㄹ수록?
faq.a: No. 먹을수록 alone is correct. Adding -(으)면 (먹으면 먹을수록) just adds emphasis and sounds a little more conversational.

intro: -든지 (-deunji) means "whether ... or" or "either ... or". It lists choices and shows that it does not really matter which one is picked. After question words it means "any-", as in 뭐든지 (anything) and 언제든지 (anytime).
usage: -든지 gives two or more options and says any of them is fine: 버스를 타든지 택시를 타든지 하자 (Let's take either the bus or a taxi). The sentence often ends with 하다 after the last option.
-든지 말든지 means "whether you do it or not" and can sound cool or a little dismissive: 가든지 말든지 마음대로 해 (Go or don't, it's up to you).
With question words it makes "any" words: 뭐든지 (anything), 언제든지 (anytime), 누구든지 (anyone), 어디든지 (anywhere). In casual speech -든지 is often shortened to -든.

examples.en: Let's take either the bus or a taxi.

examples.context: Telling a friend it's their choice
examples.en: Go or don't, do whatever you want.
I eat anything.
Feel free to contact me anytime.

compare.note: -거나 simply means "or" between options. -든지 adds the feeling that it does not matter which option is chosen.
-던지 (with 던) is a different ending about the past, as in 얼마나 춥던지 (it was so cold). Learners and even native speakers often mix up the spelling.

mistakes: Writing 던지 when you mean "whether/or." For choices, the correct spelling is 든지.

faq.q: What is the difference between 든지 and 던지?
faq.a: 든지 is about choice ("whether ... or," "any"). 던지 looks back on a past experience, usually to show how strong it was. They sound similar, so check the spelling.

faq.q: What does 언제든지 mean?
faq.a: 언제든지 means "anytime, whenever." 언제든지 연락하세요 means "Contact me anytime."

faq.q: Is 든 the same as 든지?
faq.a: Yes. 든 is a shorter, casual form of 든지, as in 뭐든 괜찮아 (Anything is fine).

intro: -거나 (-geona) means "or" between two actions or descriptions. You attach it to a verb or adjective stem to give options, like "I watch a movie or rest."
usage: -거나 connects two actions or states where either one (or both) can be true: 주말에 영화를 보거나 쉬어요 (On weekends I watch movies or rest).
You can list several options with -거나 and finish with 하다: 책을 읽거나 음악을 듣거나 해요 (I read or listen to music, that kind of thing).
-거나 itself is neutral. Politeness comes from the ending at the end of the sentence. To say "or" between two nouns, use the particle (이)나 instead.

examples.en: On weekends I watch movies or rest.
Rest if you're sick or tired.
When I'm bored, I read or go for a walk.

examples.context: Asking a friend to get in touch
examples.en: Call me or text me.

compare.note: (이)나 means "or" between nouns (커피나 차). -거나 is for verbs and adjectives (커피를 마시거나 차를 마셔요).
-든지 also lists options but adds "it doesn't matter which." -거나 is the plain, everyday "or."

mistakes: Using -거나 with nouns. Say 커피나 차, not 커피거나 차.

faq.q: What is the difference between 거나 and 나 in Korean?
faq.a: -거나 attaches to verb and adjective stems (보거나, 먹거나). (이)나 attaches to nouns (사과나 바나나). Both mean "or."

faq.q: Can I use -거나 in the past tense?
faq.a: Yes. Add it after 았/었: 집에 갔거나 자고 있을 거예요 (He probably went home or is sleeping). Often the past is only marked at the end of the sentence, though.

intro: -아도/어도 (-ado/-eodo) means "even if" or "even though". The first part does not change the result in the second part: "Even if it rains, I'll go."
usage: -아도/어도 says "no matter that A, B still happens." It can be about something imagined (even if it rains tomorrow) or something real (even though it's cold).
아무리 (no matter how) is often placed in front for emphasis: 아무리 먹어도 배고파요 (No matter how much I eat, I'm still hungry).

The same form appears in -아도/어도 되다, which asks or gives permission: 들어가도 돼요? (May I come in?). The ending is conjugated just like the polite -아요/어요, so if you can make 가요, 먹어요, 해요, you can make 가도, 먹어도, 해도.

examples.en: Even if it rains, I'll go.
No matter how much I eat, I'm hungry.
I'm fine even though it's cold.
Come for sure, even if you're late.

compare.note: -는데도 is only for real facts (even though I studied, I failed). -아도/어도 works for both real facts and imagined situations.
-지만 simply means "but" and contrasts two facts. -아도/어도 stresses that the first part does not change the outcome.
-(으)면 means "if": the result depends on the condition. -아도/어도 means the result happens anyway.

mistakes: Attaching 아도 straight to a noun. Say 학생이어도 (or 학생이라도 in speech), not 학생아도.
Forgetting irregular stems: 춥다 becomes 추워도, and 듣다 becomes 들어도.

faq.q: What does 아무리 -아도 mean?
faq.a: It means "no matter how (much)." 아무리 바빠도 밥은 먹어요 means "No matter how busy I am, I still eat."

faq.q: What does -아도 돼요 mean?
faq.a: -아도/어도 돼요 asks for or gives permission: 앉아도 돼요? means "May I sit down?" Literally it is "Even if I sit, is it okay?"

intro: -는데도 (-neundedo) means "even though" or "despite". It describes a real situation and then something that happens against what you would expect.

formation.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

usage: -는데도 links two real facts where the second is surprising given the first: 열심히 공부했는데도 떨어졌어요 (Even though I studied hard, I failed).
It often carries a feeling of frustration or surprise. It is built from -는데 (background) + 도 (even), so it follows the same conjugation as -는데.
The second part is usually a statement of fact, not a request or a suggestion. The politeness level comes from the final ending.

examples.en: Even though I studied hard, I failed.
Even though it's the weekend, I'm going to the office.
Even though I took medicine, I'm not getting better.
I've told him several times, but he doesn't listen.

compare.note: -아도/어도 can describe imagined situations (even if it rains). -는데도 is for things that are actually true.
-는데 just gives background or a soft contrast. Adding 도 makes it a clear "even though."

mistakes: Using 는데도 with adjectives. Say 비싼데도, not 비싸는데도.

faq.q: What is the difference between -는데도 and -아도?
faq.a: Both can mean "even though." -는데도 is used for facts that are really true, while -아도/어도 can also be used for "even if" about things that have not happened.

faq.q: Is -는데도 formal or casual?
faq.a: Neither on its own. 먹었는데도 배고파 is casual and 먹었는데도 배고파요 is polite. The final ending decides.

intro: -다면 (-damyeon) means "if" for situations that are imagined or less likely, like "if I won the lottery" or "if I were you". It is more hypothetical than the everyday -(으)면.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

usage: -다면 sets up an imagined or unlikely condition: 시간이 있다면 여행하고 싶어요 (If I had time, I'd like to travel). Compared with -(으)면, it sounds more "what if."
With the past tense, -았/었다면 talks about how things might have gone differently: 그때 알았다면 말했을 거예요 (If I had known then, I would have told you).
(이)라면 after a noun is very common: 내가 너라면 (if I were you). The final ending decides whether the sentence is casual or polite.

examples.en: If I were you, I wouldn't go.
If I had time, I'd like to travel.
If I had known then, I would have told you.
If you won the lottery, what would you do?

compare.note: -(으)면 is the general "if/when" for real and likely situations (비가 오면 집에 있을게요). -다면 leans toward imagined or unlikely ones.
-았/었더라면 is only about the past and carries stronger regret (if only I had). -았/었다면 is similar but a bit more neutral.

mistakes: Using the adjective form with verbs. Say 간다면 or 먹는다면, not 가다면 or 먹다면.

faq.q: What is the difference between 다면 and 면 in Korean?
faq.a: Both mean "if." -(으)면 is everyday and works for likely situations. -다면 makes the condition sound more hypothetical, like English "if I were" or "suppose."

faq.q: Does 라면 always mean ramen?
faq.a: No. After a noun, (이)라면 means "if it is" or "if (I) were," as in 나라면 (if it were me). The noodle 라면 is a different word that just sounds the same.

intro: -았/었더라면 (-at/eotdeoramyeon) means "if I had (done)". It imagines a different past, usually with regret or relief: "If I had left earlier, I wouldn't have been late."
usage: Use -았/었더라면 to talk about something that did not happen in the past and how things would have turned out. It often sounds like regret: "if only."
The second half usually ends with -았/었을 거예요 (would have) or -았/었을 텐데 (it would have been ..., but). 좋았을 텐데 (it would have been nice) is very common.
The past marker 았/었 is always part of this pattern. The politeness level comes from the last ending of the sentence.

examples.en: If I had left early, I wouldn't have been late.
It would have been nice if I'd brought an umbrella.
If I'd studied a little more, I would have passed.

examples.context: Missing a friend at a party
examples.en: If you had been there, it would have been fun.

compare.note: -았/었다면 has almost the same meaning. -았/었더라면 tends to sound more emotional, often with regret.
-(으)ㄹ걸 (I should have) is a short, sentence-final way to express regret. -았/었더라면 sets up a whole "if ... then ..." sentence.

mistakes: Dropping the past marker. Say 갔더라면, not 가더라면.

faq.q: What is the difference between 았더라면 and 았다면?
faq.a: They both mean "if I had." -았/었더라면 usually sounds more regretful and is especially common when looking back on your own mistakes.

faq.q: How do I say "I would have" after -았/었더라면?
faq.a: Use -았/었을 거예요 (would have) or -았/었을 텐데 (it would have ..., but). For example, 알았더라면 갔을 거예요 means "If I had known, I would have gone."

intro: -(으)려면 (-(eu)ryeomyeon) means "if you want to" or "in order to". It names a goal, and the second half says what is needed to reach it: "To get to City Hall, how should I go?"
usage: -(으)려면 is short for -(으)려고 하면 ("if you intend to"). The first half is a goal, and the second half is usually a requirement or advice: -아/어야 해요 (have to), 필요해요 (you need), 좋아요 (it's good to).
It is very useful for asking directions and how-to questions: 이거 사려면 어디로 가야 돼요? (Where do I go to buy this?).
The pattern is neutral. Use a polite ending like 해요 with strangers and a casual one like 해 with friends.

examples.en: How do I get to City Hall?
To lose weight, you have to exercise.
To buy a ticket, you have to wait in line.
If we don't want to be late, we need to leave now.

compare.note: -(으)려고 states your purpose (I came here to study). -(으)려면 sets up a condition and is followed by what is needed (if you want to study, you need ...).
-(으)면 is a plain "if." -(으)려면 is specifically "if you want to (do)."

mistakes: Spelling it 할려면 or 갈려면 as it is often pronounced. The standard spelling is 하려면 and 가려면.

faq.q: What is the difference between 려면 and 려고?
faq.a: -(으)려고 explains why you do something (I'm saving money to travel). -(으)려면 says what it takes to do something (to travel, you need money).

faq.q: What usually comes after -(으)려면?
faq.a: Usually a need or advice: -아/어야 해요/돼요 (have to), 필요해요 (you need), or -는 게 좋아요 (it's best to).

intro: -(으)ㄹ 테니까 (-(eu)l tenikka) means "since I will" or "since it will probably be, so". It gives either your own plan or your guess as the reason for what comes next, often a request or suggestion.
usage: Use 1, your intention: when the subject is "I," it means "I'll do this, so you ...": 내가 할 테니까 쉬어 (I'll do it, so you rest). It sounds caring or take-charge.
Use 2, a guess: with other subjects it means "it will probably be ..., so": 밖은 추울 테니까 코트 입어 (It'll probably be cold out, so wear a coat).
The second half is very often a command, request, or suggestion. In casual speech the 까 is sometimes dropped (할 테니). The final ending sets the politeness.

examples.en: I'll do it, so you rest.
It'll be cold out, so wear a coat.
I'll wait, so take your time.
They've probably arrived by now, so try calling.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 텐데 also guesses (it would be ...), but it leads to worry, contrast, or regret. -(으)ㄹ 테니까 gives a reason, usually for a request.
-(으)니까 gives a reason based on a fact. -(으)ㄹ 테니까 gives a reason based on a plan or a guess about what will be.

mistakes: Expecting it to be a promise when someone else is the subject. Only with "I" (내가/제가) does it mean "I will"; with other subjects it is a guess, like 친구가 올 테니까 (my friend will probably come, so).

faq.q: What does 테니까 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 테니까 comes after -(으)ㄹ and means "since (I) will" or "since (it) will probably be, so." For example, 제가 갈 테니까 기다리세요 means "I'll go, so please wait."

faq.q: What is the difference between 테니까 and 텐데?
faq.a: Both include a guess or plan. -(으)ㄹ 테니까 is a reason that leads to a request or suggestion. -(으)ㄹ 텐데 sets up a contrast or worry, like "it would be ..., but."

intro: -는 대신에 (-neun daesine) means "instead of (doing)" or "in exchange for". It either replaces one action with another or balances one thing against another, like "It's expensive, but it's tasty to make up for it."

formation.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

usage: Meaning 1, replacing: "instead of A, B." 택시를 타는 대신에 걸어갔어요 (Instead of taking a taxi, I walked).

Meaning 2, trading off: "A, and in return/on the other hand B." 이 집은 비싼 대신에 맛있어요 (This place is pricey, but it's tasty to make up for it). This is the meaning used with adjectives, and for deals between people: 내가 밥 사는 대신에 네가 커피 사 (I'll pay for the meal, you get the coffee).
The 에 is optional: 대신 and 대신에 mean the same. The final ending decides politeness.

examples.en: Instead of taking a taxi, I walked.
This place is pricey, but it's tasty.

examples.context: Splitting a bill with a friend
examples.en: I'll pay for the meal, you get the coffee.
I'll rest today and come early tomorrow instead.

compare.note: -지 말고 means "don't do A, do B" and is used for advice or commands. -는 대신에 can describe what happened or a trade-off, not only instructions.
-기는 하다 admits something before a "but" (it is cheap, but ...). -(으)ㄴ 대신에 balances a downside with an upside.

mistakes: Using 는 with adjectives. Say 비싼 대신에, not 비싸는 대신에.

faq.q: What is the difference between 대신 and 대신에?
faq.a: There is no real difference. 에 is optional, and 대신 alone is very common in speech.

faq.q: Can I use 대신 with a noun?
faq.a: Yes. Put it right after the noun: 밥 대신에 빵을 먹었어요 means "I ate bread instead of rice."

meaning: while I'm at it, since I'm
intro: -(으)ㄴ/는 김에 (-(eu)n/neun gime) means "while I'm at it" or "since I'm (doing it) anyway". You use the chance of one action to also do something else.

formation.example: 가다 → 가는 김에, 만들다 → 만드는 김에

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel (already done)
Verb stem ending in a consonant (already done)

usage: -(으)ㄴ/는 김에 says "since I'm doing A anyway, I'll also do B." The second action was not the original plan; the first one just made it convenient.
Use -는 김에 when the first action is happening or about to happen, and -(으)ㄴ 김에 when it has already happened: 나온 김에 (since we're already out).
It only goes with verbs. The set phrase 말 나온 김에 (since it came up) is very common in conversation. Politeness comes from the final ending.

examples.en: Since you're going to the store, grab some milk.
Since we're out anyway, let's take a walk.
Since it came up, let me ask.
While cleaning, I tidied my room too.

compare.note: -는 길에 means "on the way" while physically going somewhere. -는 김에 is about using the chance of any action, not only travel.
-(으)면서 just means two actions happen at the same time. -는 김에 adds that the second action happens because the first gave a good chance.

mistakes: Using it with adjectives, like 예쁜 김에. It only works with action verbs.
Using it for something that was the main plan. The part after 김에 should be an extra thing you add on.

faq.q: What does 말 나온 김에 mean?
faq.a: It means "since we're on the subject" or "speaking of which." People use it to bring up something related that they wanted to say.

faq.q: What is the difference between 김에 and 길에?
faq.a: -는 길에 is "on the way (somewhere)." -(으)ㄴ/는 김에 is "while I'm at it," for any action that gives you the chance to do something else.

intro: -아서/어서 그런지 (-aseo/eoseo geureonji) means "maybe because" or "perhaps it's because". You give a likely reason for something but are not completely sure it is the real cause.

formation.example: 마시다 → 마셔서 그런지, 춥다 → 추워서 그런지

usage: -아서/어서 gives a reason, and 그런지 ("whether it's because of that") makes it a guess: 피곤해서 그런지 머리가 아파요 (Maybe because I'm tired, I have a headache).
It is a soft, natural way to explain things you notice in yourself or around you. On its own, 그래서 그런지 means "maybe that's why."
Like plain -아서/어서, the reason part normally does not take the past marker 았/었. Politeness depends on the final ending.

examples.en: Maybe because I'm tired, my head hurts.
Maybe because it's the weekend, there are lots of people.
Maybe because I drank a lot of coffee, I can't sleep.
Maybe because the weather's cold, I caught a cold.

compare.note: Plain -아서/어서 states the reason as a fact. Adding 그런지 makes it a guess: "maybe because."
-기 때문에 states a clear, definite cause. -아서/어서 그런지 is softer and less certain.

mistakes: Adding the past marker to the reason part. Say 늦게 자서 그런지, not 늦게 잤어서 그런지, even when talking about last night.

faq.q: What does 그래서 그런지 mean?
faq.a: 그래서 그런지 means "maybe that's why." It follows something you just said and suggests it might be the cause of what comes next.

faq.q: Is -아서/어서 그런지 polite?
faq.a: The pattern itself is neutral. 피곤해서 그런지 졸려요 is polite and 피곤해서 그런지 졸려 is casual.

intro: -는지 (-neunji) means "whether", "if", or a question word like "where" or "what" placed inside a bigger sentence. It turns a question into part of a sentence, as in "I don't know if it's tasty" or "Do you know where he's going?"
usage: -는지 is usually followed by verbs like 알다 (know), 모르다 (not know), 궁금하다 (wonder), and 물어보다 (ask): 맛있는지 모르겠어요 (I'm not sure if it's tasty).
With question words it makes "where/what/who ..." clauses: 어디에 가는지 알아요? (Do you know where he's going?).
얼마나 -는지 몰라요 is a common expression meaning "you have no idea how (much) ...": 얼마나 맛있는지 몰라요 (You have no idea how good it is). Politeness comes from the final verb.

examples.en: Do you know where he's going?
I'm not sure if it's tasty.
Do you know who that person is?
I asked if she had eaten.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ지 is for future or uncertain things (I don't know if it will rain). -는지 is for present or past facts.
-든지 means "whether ... or, it doesn't matter which." -는지 asks or wonders about something.

mistakes: Using 는지 with adjectives. Say 비싼지 and 좋은지, not 비싸는지 and 좋는지.

faq.q: What does 얼마나 -는지 몰라요 mean?
faq.a: It means "you have no idea how (much) ..." and is used to emphasize a feeling. 얼마나 보고 싶었는지 몰라요 means "You don't know how much I missed you."

faq.q: When do I use -는지 vs -(으)ㄴ지?
faq.a: Use -는지 with action verbs and with 있다/없다. Use -(으)ㄴ지 with adjectives (비싼지, 좋은지) and 인지 with nouns.

intro: -는 것 같다 (-neun geot gatda) means "I think" or "it seems" and is used to share a guess or a soft opinion. Literally it is "it seems like the thing that is ...". Koreans use it all the time to sound less direct, even about their own opinions.

formation.example: 바쁘다 → 바쁜 것 같아요, 좋다 → 좋은 것 같아요

usage: Use it when you are guessing from what you see or hear ("it seems to be raining") or when you want to give your opinion gently ("I think it's a bit expensive").

It makes you sound modest and polite, so it is very common in conversation, interviews and customer service. Koreans even use it about their own feelings, like 좋은 것 같아요 ("I think I like it"), to avoid sounding too blunt.
The ending changes with the situation: 같아요 is polite, 같아 is casual with friends, and 같습니다 is formal. The part before 것 (는, ㄴ/은, 인) shows the tense and whether the word is a verb, adjective or noun.

examples.en: It seems to be raining outside.

examples.context: Trying on clothes with a friend
