examples.en: I think these clothes are a bit small.
I think Minsu already went home.
I think the food here is good.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is a guess about what will happen or something you can't see yet (비가 올 것 같아요, "it looks like it will rain"), while -는 것 같다 is about what is happening now (비가 오는 것 같아요, "it seems to be raining").
-나 보다 is a guess based on a clue you just noticed and is used about other people or situations, not your own opinion. -는 것 같다 works for both guesses and opinions.

mistakes: Using 는 with adjectives: 예쁘는 것 같아요 is wrong. Adjectives take (으)ㄴ, so say 예쁜 것 같아요.
Using 간 것 같아요 when you mean "is going". 간 is past ("seems to have gone"); for now, use 가는 것 같아요.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 것 같아요 so much?
faq.a: It softens what you say. Stating an opinion directly can feel strong in Korean, so people add 것 같아요 to sound humble and polite, even when they are quite sure.

faq.q: What is the difference between 는 것 같아요 and ㄹ 것 같아요?
faq.a: 는 것 같아요 is a guess about the present ("it seems to be ..."), and ㄹ 것 같아요 is a guess about the future or something not yet seen ("it looks like it will ...").

faq.q: How do I say "I don't think so" with this pattern?
faq.a: Put the negative before 것: 아닌 것 같아요 ("I don't think it is") or 안 오는 것 같아요 ("it doesn't seem to be coming").

meaning: it looks like it will, I think
intro: -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 (-(eu)l geot gatda) means "it looks like it will" or "I think it will". You use it to guess about the future or about something you haven't seen yet. It also shows up in strong feelings, like "I feel like I'm going to die of hunger".

formation.rule: no extra ㄹ, just + 것 같다
ㅂ becomes 우 + ㄹ 것 같다

usage: Use it for predictions: the weather, how a movie will be, whether someone will come. It sounds softer than saying something will definitely happen.
It also describes what you feel is about to happen to you: 배고파서 죽을 것 같아요 ("I'm so hungry I could die") or 울 것 같아요 ("I think I'm going to cry").
Like other 것 같다 forms, use 같아요 for polite speech, 같아 with close friends, and 같습니다 in formal situations.

examples.en: It looks like it'll rain tomorrow.
I'm so hungry I could die.
This movie looks like it'll be fun.
I think the exam will be hard.

compare.note: -는 것 같다 guesses about what is happening now (비가 오는 것 같아요, "it seems to be raining"); -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 guesses about what will happen (비가 올 것 같아요, "it looks like it will rain").
-(으)ㄹ 거예요 sounds more certain ("it will rain"), while -(으)ㄹ 것 같아요 adds "I think" and sounds softer.
-겠- is a quick reaction to what is in front of you (맛있겠다! "that looks delicious!"). -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is a more thought-out guess.

mistakes: Adding an extra 을 to ㄹ stems: 만들을 것 같아요 is wrong. Say 만들 것 같아요.
Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular change: 춥을 것 같아요 is wrong. Say 추울 것 같아요.

faq.q: What does 죽을 것 같아 mean?
faq.a: Literally "I think I'm going to die", but it is an everyday exaggeration meaning "I'm dying" or "this is too much", as in 배고파서 죽을 것 같아 ("I'm starving").

faq.q: Is ㄹ 것 같아요 the same as ㄹ 거예요?
faq.a: Both talk about the future, but ㄹ 것 같아요 is a softer guess ("I think it will"), and ㄹ 거예요 sounds more sure ("it will").

intro: -나 보다 and -(으)ㄴ가 보다 (-na boda / -(eu)n-ga boda) mean "it seems" or "it must be", a guess you make from something you just noticed. If you see wet umbrellas, you might say 비가 오나 봐요 ("it must be raining"). In conversation it almost always appears as 나 봐요 or 나 봐.

formation.example: 자다 → 자나 봐요, 없다 → 없나 봐요

usage: Use it when you have a clue: something you saw, heard or noticed. You are drawing a conclusion, like a small detective: "the lights are off, so nobody must be home."

It is mostly about other people and situations. You usually can't use it for your own feelings, because you already know them. You can use it about yourself when you only just realized something, like 제가 피곤했나 봐요 ("I guess I was tired").
Say 나 봐요 to people you speak politely to and 나 봐 with friends. In casual speech many people also use 나 봐 with adjectives (바쁘나 봐), but ㄴ가 보다 is the textbook form.

examples.en: It must be raining outside.

examples.context: When a friend doesn't text back
examples.en: Jisu must be really busy.
Looks like nobody's home.
You must have gone to bed late last night.

compare.note: -는 것 같다 can be a guess or your own opinion ("I think it's good"). -나 보다 is only a guess based on a clue, so you can't use it to give your opinion.
-겠- is an instant reaction to what's right in front of you (맛있겠다, "looks tasty"). -나 보다 is a conclusion drawn from evidence (맛있나 봐요, "it must be good, everyone's ordering it").

mistakes: Using it for your own current feelings: 저는 배고픈가 봐요 sounds strange. Say 배고파요 or 배고픈 것 같아요.
Writing 보아요 or 보요. The polite form is contracted to 봐요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 나 봐요 and 것 같아요?
faq.a: 나 봐요 is a guess based on something you noticed, mostly about others. 것 같아요 is broader: it works for guesses and for your own opinions.

faq.q: Why does 보다 (to see) mean "it seems" here?
faq.a: Here 보다 is used as a helper word meaning roughly "to judge from what I see". The whole pattern is learned as one unit meaning "it seems".

faq.q: When do I use 나 보다 and when ㄴ가 보다?
faq.a: Use 나 보다 with action verbs, 있다/없다 words and past tense. Use (으)ㄴ가 보다 with adjectives and 인가 보다 with nouns.

intro: -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 (-(eu)n jeogi itda) means "have (ever) done" and talks about past experiences. 적 means "a time (when)", so 간 적이 있어요 is literally "there is a time when I went". Change 있다 to 없다 to say "have never done".

formation.rule: ㄷ becomes ㄹ + 은 적이 있다

usage: Use it to ask or talk about experiences: travel, food you've tried, things that happened once. It is the Korean way to say "Have you ever ...?"
It is very often combined with -아/어 보다 ("try"): 가 본 적이 있어요 ("I've been there"), 먹어 본 적이 있어요 ("I've tried eating it"). This sounds a bit more natural for experiences you chose to try.
In casual speech the 이 is often dropped (본 적 있어?), and with 한 번도 ("not even once") the 이 often changes to 도 or 은/는 for emphasis. Use 있어요/없어요 politely and 있어/없어 with friends.

examples.en: Have you ever been to Korea?
I've never made kimchi.
Have you ever heard this song?
I've never been late, not even once.

compare.note: 가 봤어요 ("I've been / I tried going") is a shorter way to talk about experience. -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 puts more focus on "at some point in my life".
The plain past (갔어요, "I went") reports a specific event. -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다 asks or tells whether something has ever happened at all.

mistakes: Using it for everyday routines: 아침을 먹은 적이 있어요 ("I have had the experience of eating breakfast") sounds odd. Save it for experiences that are worth mentioning.
Using the present form 가는 적이 있어요. Experience is past, so use 간 적이 있어요.

faq.q: How do I say "I have never ..." in Korean?
faq.a: Use -(으)ㄴ 적이 없다: 가 본 적이 없어요 means "I've never been there". Add 한 번도 for "never once": 한 번도 본 적이 없어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 본 적 있어요 and 봐 본 적 있어요?
faq.a: 본 적 있어요 means "I've seen it". Adding -아/어 보다 (봐 본) stresses trying it out, like "I've tried watching it". For most things, 본 적 있어요 is the natural choice.

faq.q: Can I drop 이 in 적이 있다?
faq.a: Yes. In casual speech 적 있어? and 적 없어 are very common.

intro: -기로 하다 (-giro hada) means "decide to" or "agree to" do something. It is usually in the past, 기로 했어요 ("I decided to"), because a decision is something you already made. It also describes plans you agreed on with someone else.

formation.example: 가다 → 가기로 했어요, 먹다 → 먹기로 했어요

formation.rule: 안 + verb + 기로 하다, or + 지 않기로 하다
formation.example: 마시다 → 안 마시기로 했어요, 마시지 않기로 했어요

usage: Use it for decisions and resolutions: starting a diet, quitting a job, going on a trip. 했어요 means the decision is already made.
It also covers plans agreed between people. 친구랑 만나기로 했어요 means "my friend and I made plans to meet".
In the present, 기로 해요 often means "let's agree to": 우리 매일 연락하기로 해요 ("let's agree to keep in touch every day"). Use 했어요 politely and 했어 with friends.

examples.en: I've decided to start working out tomorrow.
I made plans to meet a friend on Saturday.
I've decided not to drink anymore.
I decided to quit my job.

compare.note: -(으)려고 하다 is an intention or plan ("I'm planning to"), which may still change. -기로 하다 means you have actually made the decision or agreed on it.
-기로 하다 is your own choice. -게 되다 means it happened because of circumstances ("it turned out that I'm going").

mistakes: Using 기로 해요 to mean "I decided". In the present it usually means "let's agree to". To report a decision, say 기로 했어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 기로 했어요 and 려고 해요?
faq.a: 기로 했어요 means the decision is made ("I decided to"). 려고 해요 means you intend or plan to ("I'm going to try to"), which is less firm.

faq.q: Can 기로 하다 mean a promise?
faq.a: Yes. When two people decide together, it means they agreed or promised: 같이 가기로 했잖아 ("we agreed to go together, remember?").

meaning: end up, come to, get to
intro: -게 되다 (-ge doeda) means "end up doing", "come to do" or "get to do". It shows that something happened because of circumstances or over time, not simply because you chose it. It is also a polite, humble way to share news, like 결혼하게 됐어요 ("I'm getting married").

formation.example: 가다 → 가게 됐어요, 먹다 → 먹게 됐어요

usage: Use it when a change came from outside: a new job, a transfer, a change of plans. 다음 달에 이사하게 됐어요 suggests "it worked out that I'm moving", not just "I decided to move".
It also describes how you gradually came to feel or do something: 좋아하게 됐어요 ("I came to like it"), 알게 됐어요 ("I found out, I got to know").
Koreans often announce good news with it because it sounds modest. Use 됐어요 in polite speech, 됐어 with friends and 되었습니다 in formal speech.

examples.en: It turns out I'm moving to Seoul next month.
I came to love Korean because of dramas.
How did you get to know that person?
Something came up, so I can't make it.

compare.note: -기로 하다 is a decision you made yourself. -게 되다 means it happened because of circumstances, or you are humbly presenting it that way.
For adjectives, use -아/어지다 to say "become": 추워졌어요 ("it got cold"). -게 되다 is mainly used with verbs.
-고 말다 stresses that something ended up happening in a regrettable way. -게 되다 is neutral.

mistakes: Using -게 되다 with adjectives to mean "became": 예쁘게 됐어요 sounds unnatural. Say 예뻐졌어요.
Writing 되요 instead of 돼요. The polite form of 되다 is 돼요, and the past is 됐어요.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 하게 됐어요 when sharing news?
faq.a: It sounds modest, as if things just worked out, rather than bragging about a choice. 회사에 다니게 됐어요 is a humble way to say "I got a job at a company".

faq.q: What does 알게 됐어요 mean?
faq.a: It means "I found out" or "I got to know (someone)". It is one of the most common uses of this pattern.

intro: -아지다/어지다 (-ajida / -eojida) means "become" or "get" when added to an adjective. 춥다 means "to be cold", and 추워지다 means "to get cold". It describes a change in state, like the weather, a skill or how someone looks.
usage: Add it to adjectives to show change: 좋아지다 ("get better"), 커지다 ("get bigger"), 바빠지다 ("get busy"). It follows the same vowel rules as the polite present -아요/어요.
-지다 is written attached to the word before it (좋아지다, not 좋아 지다), and then conjugated like any verb: 좋아져요, 좋아졌어요, 좋아질 거예요.
With some action verbs, -아/어지다 makes a passive meaning instead, like 만들어지다 ("be made") or 지워지다 ("be erased"). As a beginner, focus on the adjective use first.

examples.en: It's gotten a lot colder.
Korean has gotten easier for me lately.
You got so pretty!
The room is clean now.

compare.note: -게 되다 is mostly used with verbs for things that happen through circumstances ("end up doing"). For an adjective changing, use -아/어지다.
-아/어 가다/오다 shows a gradual, ongoing change. They can be combined: 추워져요 is "it gets cold", 추워지고 있어요 is "it's getting colder".

mistakes: Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular change: 춥어졌어요 is wrong. Say 추워졌어요.
Writing a space: 좋아 졌어요 is wrong. It is one word, 좋아졌어요.

faq.q: What does 좋아졌어요 mean?
faq.a: It means "it got better" or "it has improved". It is 좋다 (good) + -아지다 (become) in the polite past.

faq.q: Is 예뻐졌다 a compliment?
faq.a: Yes. 예뻐졌다 or 예뻐졌어요 means "you've gotten prettier" and is a common, friendly compliment when you haven't seen someone in a while.

meaning: make someone do, let someone do
intro: -게 하다 (-ge hada) means "make someone do" or "let someone do" something. 엄마가 저를 일찍 자게 했어요 means "My mom made me go to bed early." With an adjective it means "make something or someone (feel) a certain way", like 행복하게 하다 ("make happy").

formation.example: 가다 → 가게 해요, 먹다 → 먹게 했어요

usage: Use it when one person causes or allows another to do something. The person who is made to act usually takes 을/를 or 한테/에게: 아이를 자게 했어요, 아이한테 책을 읽게 했어요.
Depending on context, it can mean forcing ("made me clean") or allowing ("let me go"). With 못 in front, it means "not let": 못 가게 해요 ("won't let me go").
Korean also has short causative verbs like 먹이다 ("feed") and 웃기다 ("make laugh"). -게 하다 works with almost any verb, so it is the easy, flexible option. Use 해요 politely and 해 casually.

examples.en: My mom made me go to bed early.
Sorry for keeping you waiting.
My dad won't let me play games.
You make me happy.

compare.note: -게 하다 is causing someone to do something ("make them do"). -게 되다 is ending up doing something yourself because of circumstances.
-게 만들다 also means "make someone do" but often feels stronger, as if pushing someone into it or causing an unwanted result: 화나게 만들었어요 ("you made me angry").

mistakes: Mixing it up with the adverb 게, as in 예쁘게 ("prettily"). In -게 하다 the 게 is followed by 하다 and means someone is caused to do or be something.

faq.q: What does 기다리게 해서 미안해요 mean?
faq.a: It means "Sorry for keeping you waiting", literally "sorry because I made you wait". It is a very common polite apology.

faq.q: How do I say "don't let him go"?
faq.a: Use 못 + verb + 게 하다 with a command: 못 가게 하세요 ("don't let him go") or casually 못 가게 해.

intro: -(으)ㄹ 뻔하다 (-(eu)l ppeonhada) means "almost" or "nearly" did something, but it didn't actually happen. 넘어질 뻔했어요 means "I almost fell". It is almost always used in the past tense, 뻔했어요.
usage: Use it for near-misses: almost missing the bus, almost dropping your phone, almost crying. The thing did NOT happen, and usually you are relieved.
It often comes with 하마터면 ("nearly, by a hair") or 거의 ("almost") for emphasis: 하마터면 큰일 날 뻔했어요 ("that was a close call").
It is also used to exaggerate: 웃겨서 죽을 뻔했어 ("it was so funny I almost died"). Say 뻔했어요 politely and 뻔했어 to friends.

examples.en: I was almost late today.
I almost fell on the stairs.
I almost lost my wallet.
It was so funny I almost died.

compare.note: 거의 다 했어요 means "I've almost finished" (most of it is done). -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 means something nearly happened but didn't happen at all.
-고 말다 means it actually happened in the end, often sadly (넘어지고 말았어요, "I ended up falling"). -(으)ㄹ 뻔했다 means it didn't.

mistakes: Using the present tense 뻔해요 for something that almost happened. Use the past: 뻔했어요.
Using it when the thing really happened. If you did fall, say 넘어졌어요, not 넘어질 뻔했어요.

faq.q: Is 뻔하다 here the same as 뻔하다 meaning "obvious"?
faq.a: No. 뻔하다 also exists as an adjective meaning "obvious, predictable" (뻔한 이야기, "a predictable story"). After -(으)ㄹ, it means "almost".

faq.q: What does 큰일 날 뻔했다 mean?
faq.a: It means "that was a close call" or "something terrible almost happened". It is a very common phrase after a near-accident.

intro: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 (-(eu)l subakke eopda) means "have no choice but to" or "can't help but". Literally it is "there is no way except doing ...". With adjectives and observations it can also mean "it's only natural that".

formation.rule: no extra ㄹ, just + 수밖에 없다
ㅂ becomes 우 + ㄹ 수밖에 없다

usage: Use it when there was only one option: the last bus was gone, so you had to take a taxi. It explains that you didn't really choose.
With adjectives or when describing others, it means "naturally, of course": 이렇게 연습하니까 잘할 수밖에 없지 ("with that much practice, of course she's good").
It is made of 수 ("way, means") + 밖에 ("except, only") + 없다 ("there isn't"). Write 수밖에 as one word. Use 없어요 or 없었어요 politely and 없어 or 없었어 casually.

examples.en: I missed the last train, so I had to take a taxi.
If it's this good, I'll have to come back.
She practices every day, so of course she's good.
He's right, so I have to admit it.

compare.note: -아/어야 하다 means "have to" because of a rule or duty. -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 means there is simply no other option left.
-(으)ㄹ 수 없다 means "can't". Adding 밖에 flips the meaning: -(으)ㄹ 수밖에 없다 is "can only, have no choice but to".

mistakes: Reading it as "can't" because of 없다. 갈 수밖에 없어요 means "I have to go", not "I can't go".
Spacing it as 수 밖에. 밖에 is a particle here, so it attaches: 수밖에.

faq.q: Is 수밖에 없다 negative?
faq.a: No. It looks negative because of 없다, but 밖에 + 없다 together mean "only". So the meaning is "the only way is to ...", which is positive.

faq.q: Can 수밖에 없다 mean "of course"?
faq.a: Yes. When you describe a natural result, it means "it's only natural that": 비쌀 수밖에 없어요 ("of course it's expensive").

intro: -(으)ㄴ 척하다 (-(eu)n cheokhada) means "pretend". With an action verb happening now it becomes -는 척하다: 자는 척해요 ("pretends to be asleep"). With adjectives and past actions it uses -(으)ㄴ: 괜찮은 척해요 ("pretends to be okay"), 못 본 척해요 ("pretends not to have seen").

formation.example: 자다 → 자는 척해요, 알다 → 아는 척해요
보다 → 본 척해요, 먹다 → 먹은 척해요
바쁘다 → 바쁜 척해요, 괜찮다 → 괜찮은 척해요

usage: Use it when someone acts as if something is true when it is not: pretending to sleep, to be busy, to not know, to be fine.

The describing form before 척 shows timing. 먹는 척 is "pretending to eat", 먹은 척 is "pretending to have eaten". Two very common set phrases are 모르는 척하다 ("act like you don't know") and 못 본 척하다 ("pretend you didn't see").
척하다 is written attached as one word. 체하다 means the same thing (자는 체하다) but is less common in speech. Use 척해요 politely and 척해 casually.

examples.en: My little brother is pretending to be asleep.
Just pretend you don't know.
I pretended I didn't see my ex on the street.
Don't pretend you're okay.

compare.note: -(으)ㄴ 체하다 means exactly the same as -(으)ㄴ 척하다. 척하다 is more common in everyday speech.
-는 척하다 is pretending to be doing something now (자는 척, "pretending to sleep"). -(으)ㄴ 척하다 with a verb is pretending to have done it (잔 척, "pretending to have slept").

mistakes: Using 는 with adjectives: 바쁘는 척해요 is wrong. Say 바쁜 척해요.
Using the past form when you mean "pretending to be doing it": for pretending to sleep, say 자는 척해요, not 잔 척해요.

faq.q: What does 모르는 척하다 mean?
faq.a: It means "to pretend not to know" or "to act like you don't know". 모르는 척해 is "just act like you don't know".

faq.q: What does 아는 척하다 mean?
faq.a: It means "to act like you know" or "to show off what you know". It can also mean "to act like you know someone", for example greeting them on the street.

faq.q: Is it 척하다 or 척 하다?
faq.a: The standard spelling is 척하다, written as one word with the 하다 attached.

intro: -(으)ㄹ 만하다 (-(eu)l manhada) means "worth doing" or "good enough to do." You use it to recommend something, like a movie worth watching, or to say something is decent or manageable.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

usage: The most common use is a recommendation: 볼 만해요 means "it's worth watching" and 읽을 만한 책 is "a book worth reading." It sounds like a fair, honest opinion rather than wild praise.

It can also mean "good enough" or "bearable." 먹을 만해요 can mean the food is decent, and 살 만해요 means "life is okay, I'm getting by." 할 만해요 means "it's doable." Tone of voice and context tell you which sense is meant.
만하다 works like an adjective, so it becomes 만해요 (polite), 만해 (casual), and 만한 before a noun. It attaches to verbs, not to nouns or most adjectives.

examples.en: That movie is really worth watching.
Is the food here any good?
It's still good enough to use.
It's a book worth reading.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 just says something is possible. -(으)ㄹ 만하다 adds a judgment: it is worth doing or good enough to do.
This is -(으)ㄹ 만하다 added to -아/어 보다 (try). 가 볼 만해요 means "it's worth going to see," a very common way to recommend a place.

mistakes: Attaching it straight to a noun, like 영화 만해요. It needs a verb stem with the ㄹ modifier: 영화가 볼 만해요.
Treating it as strong praise. 볼 만해요 means "worth a watch," which is positive but calmer than 정말 재미있어요.

faq.q: What does 볼 만하다 mean?
faq.a: It means "worth watching" or "worth seeing." People use it to recommend movies, shows, and places, for example 그 드라마 볼 만해요.

faq.q: What does 할 만해요 mean?
faq.a: It means "it's doable" or "it's manageable." If someone asks how your new job is, 할 만해요 means it's okay, not too hard.

faq.q: Is it 볼 만하다 or 볼만하다?
faq.a: The standard spelling puts a space: 볼 만하다. Writing it together is also accepted, and you will see both online.

intro: -는 편이다 (-neun pyeonida) means "tend to" or "be on the ... side." It describes a habit or quality in a softened way, like "I tend to sleep early" or "it's fairly quiet."

formation.when: Adjective stem ending in a vowel
Adjective stem ending in a consonant

usage: 편 means "side," so the pattern literally says "it is on the side of ...". It does not state a fact flatly. It says "generally" or "compared to most," which makes it great for describing yourself or giving an opinion politely.
Koreans use it a lot when talking about themselves, because it sounds modest. 저는 잘 먹는 편이에요 ("I'm a pretty good eater") is softer than just 잘 먹어요.
With verbs, you usually need an adverb that shows degree or frequency, such as 일찍 (early), 많이 (a lot), or 자주 (often). With adjectives, no extra word is needed.
It works in any politeness level: 편이에요 (polite), 편이야 (casual), 편입니다 (formal).

examples.en: I tend to go to bed early.
This neighborhood is pretty quiet.
He's a bit of a talker.
It's not that cold today, relatively.

compare.note: -곤 하다 talks about something you used to do or do from time to time. -는 편이다 describes a general tendency or quality, often compared to other people.
-는 것 같다 is a guess ("it seems"). -는 편이다 is your judgment of degree ("it's on the ... side").

mistakes: Using a verb with no adverb, like 저는 먹는 편이에요. It sounds unfinished. Add a degree word: 저는 많이 먹는 편이에요.
Using 는 with adjectives, like 조용하는 편이에요. Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ: 조용한 편이에요.

faq.q: What does 편이에요 mean?
faq.a: It means "tend to" or "fairly, rather." 키가 큰 편이에요 means "I'm on the tall side."

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 편이다 so often?
faq.a: It softens a statement. Instead of a blunt fact, it says "generally" or "compared to others," which sounds modest and polite.

intro: -기 쉽다 (-gi swipda) means "easy to do" and -기 어렵다 (-gi eoryeopda) means "hard to do." -기 쉽다 can also mean "likely to," as in "it's easy to catch a cold in winter."
usage: -기 turns a verb into a noun ("doing"), and 쉽다 or 어렵다 describes it. You can add 가 after 기 for a little emphasis: 찾기가 어려워요.
-기 쉽다 has a second meaning: "it easily happens" or "likely to." 실수하기 쉬워요 means "it's easy to make a mistake," in the sense of "people often do."
쉽다 and 어렵다 are ㅂ-irregular, so the ㅂ changes to 우: 쉬워요, 어려워요, 쉬운, 어려운. The same pattern works with similar adjectives, like -기 힘들다 (tough to) and -기 좋다 (good for doing).

examples.en: This word is hard to memorize.
This song is easy to sing along to.
It's easy to catch a cold in winter.
It's hard to catch a taxi here.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 수 있다 says whether something is possible. -기 쉽다/어렵다 says how easy or hard it is.
-기 좋다 means "good for doing" or "nice to do," as in 걷기 좋은 날 (a nice day for a walk).

mistakes: Conjugating 쉽다 like a regular verb, as in 쉽어요. Because of the ㅂ-irregular rule, it is 쉬워요, and 어렵다 becomes 어려워요.

faq.q: How do you say "easy to" in Korean?
faq.a: Add -기 쉽다 to a verb stem: 만들기 쉬워요 means "it's easy to make." For "hard to," use -기 어렵다.

faq.q: Does 기 쉽다 always mean easy?
faq.a: No. It can also mean "likely to" or "tend to happen," like 잊어버리기 쉬워요, "it's easy to forget."

intro: -기 싫다 (-gi silta) means "I don't want to" or "I hate doing." It's how you say you really don't feel like doing something, like getting up on a Monday.
usage: -기 turns the verb into "doing," and 싫다 means "disliked" or "unwanted." Together they show a strong, emotional "I don't want to." You hear it a lot in casual speech: 가기 싫어!
싫다 describes your own feelings. For another person, Korean uses 싫어하다: 동생이 공부하기 싫어해요 ("My sibling doesn't like studying").
Even with 요, it is quite direct. To an older person or at work, -고 싶지 않아요 ("I'd rather not") sounds softer.

examples.en: I don't want to go to work on Monday.
I don't feel like doing anything today.
Even if you don't want to, you have to do your homework.
My son doesn't like eating vegetables.

compare.note: -고 싶지 않다 is a calm "I don't want to." -기 싫다 is more emotional and direct, closer to "I hate doing it."
Use 싫다 for your own feelings and 싫어하다 for someone else's. This follows the same rule as 싶다 and 싶어하다.

mistakes: Using 싫다 for another person, like 친구가 가기 싫어요. Say 친구가 가기 싫어해요 instead.
Putting 싫어요 after a noun when you mean an activity, like 공부 싫어요. That means "I hate studying (as a thing)." For "I don't want to study," say 공부하기 싫어요.

faq.q: What does 하기 싫어 mean?
faq.a: It means "I don't want to do it." It's casual and a little whiny, the kind of thing you say to friends or family.

faq.q: Is 하기 싫어요 rude?
faq.a: It isn't rude, but it is blunt. With a boss or an older person, -고 싶지 않아요 or a softer excuse usually sounds better.

intro: -(으)ㄹ까 봐 (-(eu)lkka bwa) means "in case" or "because I was worried that." It explains why you did something to avoid a possible bad outcome, or says what you are afraid of.
usage: Use it when you are afraid something might happen. Usually the next part of the sentence says what you did because of that worry: 늦을까 봐 택시를 탔어요 ("I took a taxi in case I was late"). You may also see -(으)ㄹ까 봐서 with the same meaning.
It can end a sentence too: 늦을까 봐요 or 늦을까 봐 걱정이에요 means "I'm worried I'll be late."
The second part of the sentence cannot be a command or a suggestion. For "Leave early in case you're late," use a different pattern, such as 늦을 수도 있으니까 일찍 출발하세요.

examples.context: Explaining why you took a taxi
examples.en: I took a taxi in case I was late.
I packed an umbrella in case it rains.
I didn't tell Mom because I was afraid she'd worry.
I'm worried I'll fail the exam.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ까 하다 means "I'm thinking of doing." It looks similar but is about plans, not worries.
-(으)ㄹ 것 같다 is a neutral guess ("it looks like it will"). -(으)ㄹ까 봐 adds fear or worry, and usually leads to an action you took.

mistakes: Following it with a command, like 늦을까 봐 빨리 가세요. This pattern explains your own worry, so the second part should describe what someone did or does, not an order.

faq.q: What does 할까 봐 mean?
faq.a: It means "worried that I might" or "in case." For example, 실수할까 봐 긴장했어요 means "I was nervous I might make a mistake."

faq.q: Does 봐 here mean "see"?
faq.a: It comes from 보다, but here it doesn't mean "see." The whole -(으)ㄹ까 봐 is one pattern meaning "afraid that."

intro: -(으)ㄹ까 하다 (-(eu)lkka hada) means "I'm thinking of doing" or "I might." It shares a plan you're considering but haven't firmly decided on.

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant

usage: -(으)ㄹ까 is "shall I?" and 하다 here means "to think." So 갈까 해요 is like "I'm wondering whether to go," which is a soft way to share a tentative plan.
It's used for your own plans (I or we). It sounds less certain than -(으)려고 하다, and much less certain than -기로 하다 (decided).
In the past, -(으)ㄹ까 했는데 or -(으)ㄹ까 했어요 means "I was thinking of doing it," usually followed by why it didn't happen.
It works in polite (해요), casual (해), and formal (합니다) speech.

examples.en: I'm thinking of seeing a movie this weekend.
I'm thinking of getting a haircut.
I'm thinking of learning to drive this break.
I was going to rest at home, but a friend called me out.

compare.note: -(으)려고 하다 means "I plan to" or "I'm going to" and sounds more decided. -(으)ㄹ까 하다 is still just an idea.
-기로 하다 means you have decided. Use it once the plan is settled.
-(으)ㄹ까 봐 looks similar but means "worried that" or "in case," not a plan.

mistakes: Using it for someone else's plan, like 친구가 여행 갈까 해요. For other people, report it: 친구가 여행 갈까 한대요 or 친구가 여행 가려고 해요.

faq.q: What's the difference between 할까 해요 and 하려고 해요?
faq.a: Both talk about plans. 하려고 해요 sounds like you intend to do it, while 할까 해요 sounds like you're still thinking about it.

faq.q: What does 할까 했는데 mean?
faq.a: It means "I was thinking of doing it, but..." and usually comes before the reason it didn't happen.

meaning: it is, but; I do, but
intro: -기는 하다 (-gineun hada) means "it is, but" or "I do, but." You use it to admit something is true while hinting that there's more to say, often a "but" that follows.
usage: This pattern agrees with part of something and leaves room for a "but." 맛있긴 해요 means "It IS tasty..." with a feeling that something else is coming.
It is very common with a following clause: -긴 한데, -긴 하지만. In speech, 기는 is usually shortened to 긴.
The 하다 part follows the word it attaches to. With verbs it becomes 하는데 (먹긴 하는데), and with adjectives it becomes 한데 (비싸긴 한데). In the past, both use 했는데.
You can also repeat the word instead of using 하다: 좋기는 좋은데 ("It's good, sure, but...").

examples.en: It's tasty, but a bit expensive.
I did buy the book, but I haven't read it yet.
I am tired, I'll admit.
It's nice and all, but it's too big.

compare.note: -지만 is a plain "but." -기는 하지만 adds "I admit" or "sure," so it sounds more like a partial agreement.
As a sentence ending, 잘하기는요 is a modest denial meaning "Oh, not at all." That is a different use from -기는 하다.

mistakes: Using 하는데 with adjectives, like 비싸긴 하는데. With adjectives, say 비싸긴 한데.

faq.q: What does 긴 하다 mean in Korean?
faq.a: 긴 is short for 기는. 하긴 해요 means "I do (it), but..." and 비싸긴 해요 means "it is expensive, I'll admit."

faq.q: What does 좋기는 좋은데 mean?
faq.a: It means "It's good, sure, but..." Repeating the word stresses that you agree before you add a complaint.

meaning: so much that, to the point of
intro: -(으)ㄹ 정도로 (-(eu)l jeongdoro) means "so much that" or "to the point of." It shows how strong something is by describing a result, like "I laughed so hard I cried."

formation.when: At the end of a sentence

usage: 정도 means "degree" or "extent." The part before 정도로 paints a picture of how much: 눈물이 날 정도로 웃었어요 means "I laughed to the point of tears."
It's common with everyday exaggerations, such as 죽을 정도로 ("so much I could die") and 믿을 수 없을 정도로 ("unbelievably").
To end a sentence, use 정도예요 or 정도야: 걷기 힘들 정도예요 means "It's so bad I can hardly walk."
It works in polite and casual speech; only the final verb changes.

examples.en: I ate so much I could burst.
I laughed so hard I cried.
It's so noisy I can't sleep.
She speaks Korean amazingly well.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ 만큼 means almost the same thing ("as much as, enough to") and can often replace 정도로. 정도로 tends to stress the extreme degree a bit more.
-도록 can also mean "until" or "to the point that," as in 밤새도록 (all night long), but it is more often used for "so that."

mistakes: Confusing it with 정도 after a number or noun. 한 시간 정도 means "about an hour," not "so much that." The "so much that" meaning needs a verb or adjective with -(으)ㄹ before 정도로.

faq.q: What does 정도로 mean in Korean?
faq.a: After a verb with -(으)ㄹ, it means "so much that" or "to the point of." For example, 울 정도로 아팠어요 means "It hurt so much I could have cried."

faq.q: What's the difference between 정도로 and 만큼?
faq.a: They overlap a lot and often swap freely. 정도로 leans toward describing an extreme degree, while 만큼 can also mean "as much as" in a neutral way.

meaning: as soon as; just as, the way
intro: -는 대로 (-neun daero) has two meanings: "as soon as" and "just as" or "the way." 도착하는 대로 means "as soon as I arrive," and 말한 대로 means "the way I said."

formation.when: Verb stem (as soon as, or as it is done)
Past: the way it was done (vowel stem)
Past: the way it was done (consonant stem)

usage: "As soon as": -는 대로 is used for things that will happen, so it often comes with promises, plans, or requests: 끝나는 대로 연락할게요 ("I'll call you as soon as it's done"). It is not used for one-time past events.
"Just as, the way": 시키는 대로 (the way I'm told), 본 대로 (the way I saw it), 생각한 대로 (just as I thought). With past events, use -(으)ㄴ 대로.
After a noun, 대로 is attached with no space: 계획대로 (according to plan), 마음대로 (as you like).

examples.en: I'll contact you as soon as I arrive.
I'll head over as soon as I'm done.
Try doing it the way I told you.
It turned out just as I thought.

compare.note: -자마자 also means "as soon as" and works for past events: 집에 오자마자 잤어요. -는 대로 is for future plans and requests, so 집에 오는 대로 잤어요 sounds wrong.
-(으)ㄴ 후에 just means "after" with no sense of immediacy. -는 대로 means right away.

mistakes: Using "as soon as" -는 대로 for a past event, like 도착하는 대로 전화했어요. For the past, use -자마자: 도착하자마자 전화했어요.

faq.q: What's the difference between 는 대로 and 자마자?
faq.a: Both mean "as soon as." -자마자 works for past, present, and future, while -는 대로 is used for future actions, plans, and requests.

faq.q: What does 마음대로 mean?
faq.a: It means "as you like" or "however you want." It is 마음 (heart, mind) plus 대로 (as, according to).

intro: -(으)면 좋겠다 (-(eu)myeon joketda) means "I wish" or "I hope." Literally it says "it would be good if," so 비가 오면 좋겠어요 means "I hope it rains."
usage: -(으)면 is "if" and 좋겠다 is "it would be good." Together they express a hope or a wish about yourself, another person, or a situation.
The past form -았/었으면 좋겠다 is very common and sounds a bit more heartfelt, like "I really wish." It doesn't mean the event is in the past: 빨리 방학이었으면 좋겠다 means "I wish it were vacation already."
It is also a gentle way to make a request: 와 주시면 좋겠어요 means "I'd be glad if you could come."
좋겠어요 is polite, 좋겠어 is casual, and 좋겠다 is often said to yourself, like thinking out loud.

chips.g: it would be nice, I hope (polite)

examples.en: I hope the weather is nice tomorrow.
I wish it were the weekend already.
I hope I passed the exam.
I'd appreciate it if you could wait a little longer.

compare.note: -고 싶다 is "I want to do" something myself. -(으)면 좋겠다 is a wish about any situation or person, including things outside your control.
-았/었으면 하다 means nearly the same ("I wish") and sounds a little softer and more formal.

mistakes: Using -고 싶다 for a wish about someone else, like 친구가 오고 싶어요. To say "I want my friend to come," use 친구가 왔으면 좋겠어요.

faq.q: What does 좋겠다 mean by itself?
faq.a: On its own, 좋겠다 often means "lucky you" or "that must be nice," said when someone shares good news.

faq.q: Why do Koreans say 했으면 좋겠다 with the past tense?
faq.a: The past form makes the wish feel stronger and more like a daydream. It still talks about the present or future, not the past.

intro: -(으)ㄴ 지 되다 (-(eu)n ji doeda) means "it's been (a length of time) since." 한국에 온 지 일 년 됐어요 means "It's been a year since I came to Korea."

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel
Verb stem ending in a consonant
formation.example: 먹다 → 먹은 지 두 시간 됐어요

formation.when: Verb stem ending in ㄹ (ㄹ drops)

formation.example: 만나다 → 만난 지 한 달이 지났어요

usage: Use it to say how much time has passed since something happened. The pattern is: action + (으)ㄴ 지 + amount of time + 되다. Since time has already passed, 되다 is usually in the past: 됐어요.
To ask "How long has it been since...?" or "How long have you been...?", say -(으)ㄴ 지 얼마나 됐어요? For a long time, use 오래됐어요.
지 here is written with a space: 온 지. This sets it apart from -는지 ("whether"), which is written together.
Only the last verb changes for politeness: 됐어요 (polite), 됐어 (casual), 되었습니다 (formal).

examples.en: It's been a year since I came to Korea.
How long have you been studying Korean?
It hasn't even been an hour since I ate.
It's already been 100 days since we met!

compare.note: -는지 means "whether" or "if," as in 뭐 하는지 몰라요 ("I don't know what he's doing"). It's written with no space and has nothing to do with time.
-(으)ㄴ 후에 means "after doing." -(으)ㄴ 지 되다 measures how much time has passed since.

mistakes: Using the present form -는 지, like 공부하는 지 1년 됐어요. The start happened in the past, so use -(으)ㄴ: 공부한 지 1년 됐어요.

faq.q: How do you say "How long have you been..." in Korean?
faq.a: Use -(으)ㄴ 지 얼마나 됐어요? For example, 한국에 산 지 얼마나 됐어요? means "How long have you lived in Korea?"

faq.q: Is it 온 지 or 온지?
faq.a: When it means "since," write it with a space: 온 지. Without a space, -ㄴ지 is a different ending that means "whether."

intro: -아/어 주다 (-a/eo juda) means "to do something for someone." You add it to an action verb to show that the action is a favor or a help to another person. Its polite request form, -아/어 주세요, is one of the most useful phrases in Korean: "please do this for me."
usage: 주다 on its own means "to give." When it follows another verb in the -아/어 form, it means you are giving the action itself: doing it for someone's benefit. 읽어요 is "I read," but 읽어 줘요 is "I read (it) to you / for you."

The most common use is asking for something politely: -아/어 주세요 (please do it for me). It sounds softer than a plain command with -(으)세요, because you are framing it as a favor. Casual versions with friends are -아/어 줘 (do it for me) and -아/어 줄래? (will you do it for me?).
To offer help, use -아/어 줄게(요) (I'll do it for you) or -아/어 줄까(요)? (shall I do it for you?). When you do something for an older person or a customer, Koreans switch 주다 to its humble form 드리다.

examples.en: Please wrap this up for me.
I'll buy it for you.
Could you close the window?
Please wait just a moment.

compare.note: The humble version. Use 드리다 when you do something for someone older or higher in status, like a teacher, a boss, or a customer.
A plain polite request or instruction (앉으세요, please sit). -아/어 주세요 adds the feeling of asking a favor for yourself, so it sounds a little softer.

mistakes: Using 주다 for something you do for an elder. 할머니를 도와줬어요 sounds off; say 도와드렸어요.
Mixing up noun + 주세요 and verb + 아/어 주세요. 물 주세요 means "give me water," while 물을 사 주세요 means "please buy water for me."

faq.q: What does 주세요 mean after a verb?
faq.a: After a verb in the -아/어 form, 주세요 means "please do this for me." For example, 도와주세요 is "please help me" and 와 주세요 is "please come."

faq.q: Should I write 해 주다 or 해주다?
faq.a: Both are accepted. Korean spelling rules let you write helper verbs like 주다 with or without a space, so 해 주세요 and 해주세요 are both fine. A few verbs, like 도와주다, are dictionary words and are always written together.

faq.q: How do I say "Can you do this for me?" casually?
faq.a: Use -아/어 줄래? or -아/어 줄 수 있어? with friends, for example 이거 좀 들어 줄래? (Can you hold this for me?).

intro: -아/어 드리다 (-a/eo deurida) means "to do something for someone" in a humble, respectful way. It is the polite version of -아/어 주다, used when the person you help is older or higher in status, like a parent, a teacher, a boss, or a customer.
usage: 드리다 is the humble word for "to give." Using it after a verb lowers yourself and raises the person you are helping. It is about who receives the favor, not who you are talking to.
You will hear it constantly in shops, restaurants, and customer service: 도와드릴까요? (May I help you?), 바로 보내 드릴게요 (I'll send it right away). With parents and grandparents, it shows warmth and respect.
When an older person does something for you, do not use 드리다. Use the honorific -아/어 주시다 instead: 선생님이 설명해 주셨어요 (The teacher explained it for me).

examples.en: I'll find it for you.
Shall I carry your bag for you?
I read a letter to my grandmother.
I will send it to you right away.

compare.note: The everyday form for friends, younger people, and equals. 드리다 is the humble version for elders and customers.
Used when an older person does something for you or for someone else. 드리다 is only for actions you (or others) do for the respected person.

mistakes: Using 드리다 when the elder is the one helping. Say 할아버지가 도와주셨어요, not 할아버지가 도와드렸어요 (which would mean grandpa helped someone else respected).
Using 드리다 for a younger sibling or a friend. It sounds oddly stiff; use 주다.

faq.q: What is the difference between 주다 and 드리다?
faq.a: Both mean "to give" or "to do for someone." 주다 is neutral, and 드리다 is humble, used when the receiver deserves respect, like a parent, teacher, or customer.

faq.q: What does 드릴까요 mean?
faq.a: 드릴까요? means "Shall I (do it) for you?" in a polite, humble way. 도와드릴까요? is the standard "May I help you?" in shops.

intro: -아/어 버리다 (-a/eo beorida) means "to do something completely" or "to end up doing it," with an added feeling. Depending on the situation, that feeling is regret ("oh no, it's gone"), relief ("finally, it's done"), or a decision to just get something over with.
usage: 버리다 on its own means "to throw away." As a helper verb it says the action is fully done and can't be taken back. It is mostly used in the past tense: 가 버렸어요 (it already left, it's gone).
The feeling comes from context. 케이크를 다 먹어 버렸어 can be a guilty confession. 숙제를 끝내 버렸어 sounds relieved, like a weight is off your shoulders. Without 버리다, the sentence just states the fact.
In the present or as a command, it means "just do it and be done": 그냥 말해 버려 (just say it already). It works in both casual and polite speech.

examples.en: I ate all the cake.
The bus already left.
I got all my homework done.
I ended up telling the secret.

compare.note: Also "end up," but more serious and bookish, usually about something you tried to avoid. It is not used for relief the way 버리다 can be.
놓다 means you did something and kept the result for later. 버리다 means the action is finished and gone, often with regret or relief.

mistakes: Using it to describe a neutral event. 밥을 먹어 버렸어요 is not just "I ate"; it adds "oops" or "done with it." If you just mean "I ate," say 밥을 먹었어요.
Spacing the dictionary words 잊어버리다 (to forget) and 잃어버리다 (to lose). These are single words and are written without a space.

faq.q: Does 버리다 mean "throw away" here?
faq.a: Not literally. As a helper verb it adds the idea that the action is completely finished, often with regret or relief. The original meaning of "throwing away" explains the feeling: once it's done, it's gone.

faq.q: What is the difference between -아/어 버리다 and -고 말다?
faq.a: Both can mean "ended up," but -아/어 버리다 is everyday and can show relief, while -고 말다 is more formal and usually describes an unwanted result after resisting it.

intro: -아/어 놓다 and -아/어 두다 (-a/eo nota, -a/eo duda) mean "to do something in advance" or "to do something and leave it that way." They show that you did an action and its result is kept ready for later.
usage: 놓다 means "to put down" and 두다 means "to put, to keep." After another verb, they say you did something on purpose and the result stays in place: 예약해 놨어요 (I've booked it, it's all set).
Often it means preparing ahead: buying snacks before guests come, charging your phone before a trip. It can also mean leaving something in a state: 문을 열어 놓으세요 (please leave the door open).
The two are mostly interchangeable. 두다 can feel a bit more like keeping something for a long time (기억해 두세요, keep it in mind). In speech, 놓아 shortens to 놔, so 놓았어요 is usually 놨어요.

examples.en: I've booked the restaurant.
I'll leave the window open.
Be sure to memorize this word.
Did you charge your phone?

compare.note: Describes a state with verbs that have no object: 문이 열려 있어요 (the door is open). -아/어 놓다 says someone did it on purpose: 문을 열어 놨어요 (I left the door open).
버리다 means the action is finished and gone. 놓다/두다 means the result is kept and ready to use.

mistakes: Writing 났어요 instead of 놨어요. 났어요 comes from 나다 (to come out, happen); the short form of 놓았어요 is 놨어요.
Using it with adjectives or verbs without an object. 놓다/두다 go with action verbs that act on something, like 사다, 열다, 준비하다.

faq.q: What is the difference between 놓다 and 두다?
faq.a: In most sentences they mean the same thing. 두다 can feel slightly more like keeping something for a while, and some set phrases prefer it, like 기억해 두다 (keep in mind).

faq.q: What does 해 놨어요 mean?
faq.a: 해 놨어요 means "I've done it (ahead of time)" or "I've got it done." It is the spoken short form of 해 놓았어요.

intro: -고 말다 (-go malda) means "to end up doing something," usually something you did not want or tried to avoid. It is almost always used in the past, -고 말았어요, and carries a feeling of regret or "in the end, it happened anyway."
usage: Use -고 말았다 when something happened in the end, despite effort or wishes. Words like 결국 (in the end) and 또 (again) often come with it: 결국 울고 말았어요 (I ended up crying in the end).
It sounds a bit more serious and story-like than -아/어 버리다. You will see it a lot in writing, diaries, and narration. In casual chat, people often use -아/어 버렸어 instead.
A second use is strong determination in the future: -고 말겠다 or -고 말 거야, "I will do it no matter what." This works only with your own plans.

examples.en: In the end, I ended up crying.
I ended up eating a late-night snack again.
I ended up falling asleep at my desk.
This time I'll pass no matter what.

compare.note: More common in everyday talk and can show relief as well as regret. -고 말다 sounds heavier and is mostly about unwanted results.
A neutral "end up" or "come to," with no feeling of regret. 한국에 살게 됐어요 just reports how things turned out.

mistakes: Using it with adjectives. -고 말다 goes with verbs: 늦고 말았어요 is fine, but you cannot attach it to 예쁘다 or 좋다.
Using it for a happy, everyday event. 맛있는 밥을 먹고 말았어요 sounds like eating was a defeat.

faq.q: What does 말았어요 mean?
faq.a: After a verb with -고, 말았어요 means "ended up (doing it)" with regret. On its own, 말다 means "to stop" or "not to do," as in -지 마세요.

faq.q: Can -고 말다 be positive?
faq.a: In the future form -고 말겠다 or -고 말 거야 it shows strong resolve, like "I'll do it no matter what." In the past it usually describes something you wish hadn't happened.

intro: -아/어 있다 (-a/eo itda) means "to be in a state" that continues after an action is finished. 앉다 is "to sit down," and 앉아 있다 is "to be sitting." It is used with verbs that do not take an object, like 앉다, 서다, 열리다, and 남다.

formation.example: 남다 → 남아 있다 / 서다 → 서 있다

usage: Think of it as a snapshot of the result. Someone sat down, and now they are sitting: 앉아 있어요. The door was opened, and now it is open: 문이 열려 있어요.

It only works with verbs that have no object. For a door, use the passive verb 열리다 (be opened), not 열다 (to open something): 문이 열려 있어요. If you want to say someone left it open on purpose, use -아/어 놓다 instead.
For an older person, swap 있다 for 계시다: 할머니가 앉아 계세요 (Grandma is sitting). The ending of 있다 sets the politeness, as usual: 있어 (casual), 있어요 (polite).

examples.en: She's sitting over there.
The store door is closed.
Oh, the light is on.
There's still milk left in the fridge.

compare.note: Describes an action in progress: 먹고 있어요 (I'm eating). -아/어 있다 describes the state after an action: 앉아 있어요 (I'm sitting).
Used with verbs that take an object, to show someone did it on purpose: 문을 열어 놨어요 (I left the door open).

mistakes: Using it with a verb that takes an object. 문을 열어 있어요 is wrong; say 문이 열려 있어요 (the door is open) or 문을 열어 놨어요 (I left the door open).
Using it for clothes. Wearing is 입고 있다, not 입어 있다: 코트를 입고 있어요 (I'm wearing a coat).

faq.q: What is the difference between -고 있다 and -아/어 있다?
faq.a: -고 있다 is an action happening now (I'm sitting down). -아/어 있다 is the state that remains afterward (I'm seated). With most verbs only one of them sounds natural.

faq.q: How do I say "someone is standing" in Korean?
faq.a: Use 서 있다: 친구가 밖에 서 있어요 (My friend is standing outside). 서다 + 어 shortens to 서.

intro: -아/어 가다 and -아/어 오다 (-a/eo gada, -a/eo oda) mean "to keep doing" or "to gradually become" over time. -아/어 가다 looks forward, toward the future or an end point, and -아/어 오다 looks back, at something that has continued from the past up to now.
usage: Picture the action moving along a timeline. With 가다, it moves away from now toward the future: 일이 거의 끝나 가요 (the work is nearly done, it's getting there). With 오다, it moves from the past toward now: 10년 동안 해 왔어요 (I've been doing it for 10 years).
-아/어 가다 often describes something approaching a finish or slowly changing: food getting cooked, a child growing to look like a parent. Words like 점점 (gradually) and 거의 (almost) fit well.

-아/어 오다 is common with 지금까지 (until now) and a length of time, to talk about effort or a long-running situation. Be aware that some verbs with 가다/오다 just describe movement, like 사 가다 (buy and take away) or 가져오다 (bring).

examples.en: My work is almost done.
The meat is almost cooked.
I've been doing this job for 10 years.
The child looks more and more like her dad.

compare.note: Just says an action is happening now. -아/어 가다 adds direction: it is moving toward an end or changing step by step.
Means "to become" (추워지다, get cold). It describes the change itself, while -아/어 가다/오다 stress how it continues over time. They can combine: 좋아져 가요.

mistakes: Using 가다 for something that lasted from the past until now. For "I've studied Korean for 3 years," say 3년 동안 공부해 왔어요, not 공부해 가요.

faq.q: What does 끝나 가요 mean?
faq.a: 끝나 가요 means "it's almost over" or "it's coming to an end." The 가다 shows the action is moving toward its finish.

faq.q: What is the difference between 해 왔어요 and 했어요?
faq.a: 했어요 simply says you did it. 해 왔어요 says you have kept doing it over a period of time up to now, like "I have been doing it."

intro: -고 싶어 하다 (-go sipeo hada) means "he wants to" or "she wants to." Korean uses -고 싶다 for your own wishes, and switches to -고 싶어 하다 when describing what someone else wants, since you can only see their wish from the outside.
usage: In Korean, words for wishes and feelings (싶다, 좋다, 슬프다) normally describe the speaker's own inner state. To talk about a third person, you add -아/어 하다, which describes how they show it. So 저는 가고 싶어요 (I want to go), but 동생이 가고 싶어 해요 (my sibling wants to go).
When you ask someone directly, use plain 싶다: 뭐 먹고 싶어요? (What do you want to eat?). -고 싶어 하다 is for he, she, they, and people you are talking about.
The ending on 하다 sets the politeness and tense: 싶어 해 (casual), 싶어 해요 (polite), 싶어 했어요 (wanted). For an elder, use 싶어 하세요.

examples.en: My younger sibling wants to raise a puppy.
The kids want to go to the amusement park.
Minsu missed you.
Grandpa wants to go to his hometown.

compare.note: For your own wishes, or to ask "you" directly: 뭐 하고 싶어요? -고 싶어 하다 is for other people.
The same idea for feeling words: 슬프다 (I'm sad) becomes 슬퍼하다 (he is sad). -고 싶어 하다 is this rule applied to 싶다.

mistakes: Saying 친구가 한국에 가고 싶어요 for a statement about a friend. Say 친구가 한국에 가고 싶어 해요.
Adding it to a noun. "She wants a cat" is 고양이를 갖고 싶어 해요 or 고양이를 원해요, not 고양이 싶어 해요.

faq.q: Is it 싶어 하다 or 싶어하다?
faq.a: The standard spelling is 싶어 하다 with a space, because -아/어 하다 is attached to the whole phrase -고 싶다. You will often see 싶어하다 written together online, and people understand both.

faq.q: Can I say 그는 가고 싶어요?
faq.a: It sounds unnatural as a plain statement, because 싶다 describes your own feelings. Say 그는 가고 싶어 해요. In a question to someone, 가고 싶어요? is fine.

intro: -아/어하다 (-a/eohada) turns a feeling adjective into a verb meaning "to feel that way" or "to show that feeling." It is mostly used to describe how other people feel, because Korean feeling adjectives like 슬프다 (sad) normally describe only the speaker.
usage: 저는 슬퍼요 means "I'm sad." For another person, Korean prefers 친구가 슬퍼해요 (my friend is sad, is showing sadness). The -아/어하다 form describes feelings you can see from the outside.
The new verb can take an object with 을/를: 아이가 개를 무서워해요 (the child is scared of dogs). Compare the adjective, which takes 이/가: 저는 개가 무서워요 (dogs are scary to me).
Some of these are so common they are learned as their own words: 좋아하다 (to like), 싫어하다 (to dislike), 귀여워하다 (to adore). It is written attached to the adjective, with no space.

examples.en: My friend is really sad.
Our cat hates water.
The child is scared of dogs.
Grandma adores her grandkids.

compare.note: The same rule applied to wanting: 가고 싶다 (I want to go) becomes 가고 싶어 하다 (she wants to go).
Use the adjective for your own feelings and when asking someone directly: 괜찮아요? 피곤해요?

mistakes: Using it for your own feelings in the moment. 저는 지금 슬퍼해요 sounds like you are describing yourself from outside; say 저는 지금 슬퍼요.
Keeping the wrong particle. 무섭다 takes 이/가 (개가 무서워요), but 무서워하다 takes 을/를 (개를 무서워해요).

faq.q: What is the difference between 좋다 and 좋아하다?
faq.a: 좋다 is an adjective, "to be good" or "to be liked by me": 저는 커피가 좋아요. 좋아하다 is a verb, "to like": 저는 커피를 좋아해요. Both can describe your own taste, but for other people 좋아하다 is the natural choice.

faq.q: Why is it 무서워하다 and not 무섭어하다?
faq.a: 무섭다 is an ㅂ-irregular adjective, so before 아/어 the ㅂ changes to 우 and combines into 워: 무서워요, 무서워하다. The same happens with 귀엽다 → 귀여워하다.

intro: -곤 하다 (-gon hada) means "to often do" or, in the past, "used to do." It describes something that happens again and again as a habit, and it is very often used when looking back on the past: -곤 했어요.
usage: -곤 하다 adds the idea of repetition: not one time, but something that kept happening. In the past, -곤 했어요 is close to English "used to" or "would": 어릴 때 여기서 놀곤 했어요 (I used to play here as a kid).
In the present, -곤 해요 means "I tend to" or "I sometimes": 가끔 산책하곤 해요. Time words like 가끔 (sometimes), 자주 (often), and 어릴 때 (when I was young) fit naturally.
It sounds slightly thoughtful or storytelling, so you hear it a lot when people share memories. 곤 is a short form of 고는, which you may see in writing.

examples.en: I used to play here when I was little.
When things are hard, I often listen to this song.
I sometimes go for walks on weekends.
In college I used to pull all-nighters.

compare.note: Also looks back at past habits, but it describes a noun: 자주 가던 카페 (the cafe I used to go to). -곤 하다 ends the sentence.
Means "tend to" or "rather" and describes a general tendency or personality. -곤 하다 focuses on a repeated action.

mistakes: Using it for a one-time event. 어제 영화를 보곤 했어요 sounds wrong, because -곤 하다 needs repetition. Say 어제 영화를 봤어요.
Attaching it to adjectives. Use it with action verbs, like 가다, 듣다, 먹다.

faq.q: What does 곤 했어요 mean?
faq.a: -곤 했어요 means "used to" or "would often" in the past: 주말마다 등산하곤 했어요 (I used to go hiking every weekend).

faq.q: Is -곤 하다 used in everyday speech?
faq.a: Yes, especially when talking about memories or habits, though it can sound a little thoughtful. In very casual talk people may simply say 자주 했어 (I did it often).

intro: -다고 하다 (-dago hada) means "(someone) said that" or "they say that." It is how Korean reports a statement in your own words, like English "She said she's busy" instead of quoting her exactly.

formation.example: 가다 → 간다고 해요 / 살다 → 산다고 해요

usage: Take the plain statement form (바쁘다, 간다, 먹는다, 갔다), add 고, then 하다. 하다 here means "to say." The ending of 하다 shows when it was said and how polite you are: 했어요 (said), 해요 (says, they say).
-다고 해요 in the present often means "I heard" or "they say," like passing on news or a forecast. -다고 했어요 reports what a specific person said.
In conversation, -다고 해요 is very often shortened to -대요: 바쁘대요 (she says she's busy). The future is usually -(으)ㄹ 거라고 하다: 갈 거라고 했어요 (he said he would go).

examples.en: They say it will rain tomorrow.
Minji said she's busy today.
Jisu said she already ate.
They say that restaurant is really good.

compare.note: The spoken short form of -다고 해요. 비가 온대요 and 비가 온다고 해요 mean the same thing.
Questions, suggestions, and commands each have their own quoting form. -다고 하다 is only for statements.

mistakes: Forgetting the ㄴ/는 with verbs. It is 간다고 and 먹는다고, not 가다고 or 먹다고. Adjectives stay plain: 바쁘다고.
Using 이다고 with nouns. Nouns take (이)라고: 의사라고 했어요, not 의사이다고.

faq.q: What is the difference between -다고 해요 and -대요?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. -대요 is the contracted spoken form of -다고 해요 and is more common in casual conversation.

faq.q: How do I say "He said he will go"?
faq.a: Say 간다고 했어요, or for a clearer future, 갈 거라고 했어요.

intro: -냐고 하다 (-nyago hada) means "(someone) asked if" or "asked what, where, when." It is how Korean reports a question in your own words, like "Mom asked if I ate." Instead of 하다, people often use 묻다 or 물어보다 (to ask).
usage: Turn the question into a plain question form with -냐, add 고, then 하다 (or 묻다, 물어보다). Question words stay in: 어디 사냐고 물어봤어요 (asked where I live). Without a question word, it means "asked if": 바쁘냐고 했어요 (asked if I was busy).
Even though -냐 on its own is a blunt casual question, inside a quote it is just the reporting form. The politeness of the whole sentence comes from the last verb: 물어보셨어요 is polite and respectful.
In formal writing you may see older forms: -느냐고 for verbs and -(으)냐고 for adjectives (좋으냐고). In speech, -냐고 is used for both. The spoken short form of -냐고 해요 is -냬요.

examples.en: A friend asked where I live.
Mom asked if I ate.
The team leader asked when it will be finished.
A customer asked how much this is.

compare.note: Reports a statement (said that). -냐고 하다 reports a question (asked if).
Embeds a question inside a sentence without quoting anyone: 어디 사는지 몰라요 (I don't know where she lives). -냐고 reports what someone asked.

mistakes: Keeping the ㄹ in ㄹ-stem verbs. It is 어디 사냐고 (from 살다), not 살냐고.
Using it to report an answer or a statement. 바쁘냐고 했어요 means "asked if I was busy"; "said I was busy" is 바쁘다고 했어요.

faq.q: What does 뭐 하냐고 mean?
faq.a: 뭐 하냐고 means "(someone) asked what (I'm) doing." As 뭐 하냐고요? on its own, it repeats a question: "I asked what you're doing!"

faq.q: Is -냐고 rude?
faq.a: Not inside a quote. The politeness comes from the final verb, so 선생님이 괜찮냐고 물어보셨어요 is perfectly polite.

intro: -자고 하다 (-jago hada) means "(someone) suggested that we" or "said let's." It reports a "let's" sentence in your own words: 친구가 영화 보자고 했어요 means "My friend suggested we watch a movie."
usage: Take the casual "let's" form -자, add 고, then 하다 (to say). The final verb carries tense and politeness: 가자고 했어요 (suggested going), 가자고 해요 (is suggesting going).
It always involves the original speaker doing the action together with someone else. If someone told only you to do something, use -(으)라고 하다 instead.
In speech, -자고 해요 is often shortened to -재요: 같이 가재요 (she says let's go together). Like other quoting forms, it only works with verbs.

examples.en: My friend suggested we watch a movie together.
My older sister suggested we go shopping tomorrow.
We said we'd stop fighting, remember?
A coworker asked me to go eat lunch.

compare.note: Reports a command or request to someone else: 가라고 했어요 (told me to go). -자고 하다 includes the speaker: 가자고 했어요 (suggested we go).
The direct casual "let's": 가자! -자고 하다 is how you tell someone else about that suggestion.

mistakes: Using it with adjectives. You can't suggest "let's be pretty" this way; -자고 하다 goes with action verbs.
Confusing it with -자마자 (as soon as). 먹자고 했어요 is "suggested eating," while 먹자마자 is "as soon as (I) ate."

faq.q: What does 가재요 mean?
faq.a: 가재요 is the spoken short form of 가자고 해요: "(someone) says let's go."

faq.q: How do I report "let's not"?
faq.a: Use -지 말자고 하다: 늦지 말자고 했어요 (We said let's not be late).

intro: -(으)라고 하다 (-(eu)rago hada) means "(someone) told me to" or "said to do." It reports a command or instruction in your own words: 엄마가 일찍 자라고 했어요 means "Mom told me to go to bed early."

formation.when: Verb stem ending in a vowel

usage: Use it to pass on orders, advice, and instructions. The final verb shows tense and politeness: 하라고 했어요 (told me to do it), 하라고 하셨어요 (a respected person told me to).
For "told me not to," use -지 말라고 하다: 의사가 술을 마시지 말라고 했어요 (the doctor told me not to drink).

When someone asked for something for themselves, Korean uses 달라고 instead of 주라고: 친구가 도와 달라고 했어요 (my friend asked me to help him). 주라고 is used when the favor is for a third person: 동생을 도와주라고 했어요 (told me to help my sibling). In speech, -(으)라고 해요 often shortens to -(으)래요.

examples.en: Mom told me to go to bed early.
The teacher told us to read this book.
The doctor told me not to drink.
My friend asked me to lend him some money.

compare.note: Reports a "let's" suggestion that includes the speaker. -(으)라고 하다 reports a command for someone else.
Looks similar but attaches to nouns and reports a statement: 학생이라고 했어요 (said she is a student). 읽으라고 is a command (told to read).

mistakes: Adding 으 after ㄹ stems. It is 만들라고 and 놀라고, not 만들으라고.
Using 주라고 when the person asked for themselves. 친구가 도와주라고 했어요 sounds like the friend wanted you to help someone else; say 도와 달라고 했어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 달라고 and 주라고?
faq.a: 달라고 is used when the person asks for something for themselves (give me, do it for me). 주라고 is used when they ask you to give or do something for someone else.

faq.q: What does 하라고 mean?
faq.a: 하라고 means "(told) to do it." 하라고 했잖아! is a common way to say "I told you to do it!"

intro: (이)라고 하다 ((i)rago hada) means "to be called" or "(someone) said it is." You attach it to a noun, so you can introduce your name (저는 하나라고 합니다), ask what something is called, or report that someone said "it's a ___."
usage: The most common beginner use is introducing yourself: 저는 김하나라고 합니다 (I'm called Kim Hana). It sounds a bit more modest and formal than 저는 김하나입니다.
It is also how you ask about words: 이거 한국어로 뭐라고 해요? (What do you call this in Korean?). And it reports statements about nouns: 내일이 시험이라고 했어요 (he said tomorrow is the exam).
With a direct quote in quotation marks, 라고 follows the quote: "사랑해"라고 했어요. In speech, (이)라고 해요 often shortens to (이)래요: 시험이래요 (they say it's an exam).

examples.en: My name is Kim Hana.
What do you call this in Korean?
Minho said tomorrow is the exam.
This bread is called bungeoppang.

compare.note: Reports statements with verbs and adjectives (바쁘다고 했어요). (이)라고 하다 is the version for nouns.
Reports commands with verbs: 읽으라고 했어요 (told me to read). (이)라고 attaches to nouns: 책이라고 했어요 (said it's a book).

mistakes: Using 이라고 after a vowel. It is 수지라고, not 수지이라고. Use 이라고 only after a consonant: 지민이라고.
Writing 이다고. Nouns never take 다고; the quoting form is (이)라고.

faq.q: How do you say "What is this called?" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 이거 뭐라고 해요? or, for the Korean word, 이거 한국어로 뭐라고 해요?

faq.q: What does 라고 합니다 mean in an introduction?
faq.a: 저는 ___(이)라고 합니다 means "I am called ___" or "My name is ___." It is polite and slightly humble, good for first meetings and presentations.

intro: -다고요 and -다니까요 (-dagoyo, -danikkayo) mean "I said" or "I'm telling you." You use them to repeat or insist on something you already said. -다고요? with a rising tone can also mean "You said what?" when you are surprised or checking.
usage: These endings come from quoting. When someone didn't hear you or doesn't believe you, you quote yourself: 간다고요 (I said I'm going). -다니까요 is stronger, like "I'm telling you!" or "I already said so!"
-다고요? with a rising tone checks what you heard, often with surprise: 벌써 끝났다고요? (It's already over, you said?).
The tone matters. -다니까(요) can sound frustrated or impatient, so be careful with elders and bosses. The casual versions are -다고 and -다니까 (no 요).

examples.en: I said I'm leaving now.
I'm telling you, I'm really fine.
It's already over?
I'm telling you, it wasn't me.

compare.note: Reminds someone of something they should already know (you know). -다니까요 insists on something you already said and they aren't accepting.
Shows disbelief at news: 벌써 끝났다니! (I can't believe it's already over!). -다고요? checks the news as a question.

mistakes: Using -다니까요 with a boss or an elder when you are annoyed. Even with 요, it can sound like talking back.
Forgetting the verb form. It is 간다고요 and 먹는다니까요, not 가다고요 or 먹다니까요.

faq.q: What does 다니까 mean?
faq.a: -다니까 means "I'm telling you" or "I said so already." For example, 괜찮다니까 means "I said I'm fine!" Note that -(으)니까 alone means "because," which is different.

faq.q: Is -다고요 rude?
faq.a: Not by itself. Calmly repeating with -다고요 is fine. But a sharp tone, or -다니까요 when you are annoyed, can sound impatient, especially toward elders.

intro: 도 (do) means "also" or "too" and attaches right after a noun: 저도 means "me too." With a negative verb it can also mean "even" or "not even." It is one of the first particles learners meet, and you will hear it constantly.
usage: 도 adds something to what was already said: "this one too." 저도 좋아해요 means "I like it too." It takes the place of 은/는, 이/가 and 을/를, so you never stack them together.
With 에, 에서 or 한테, 도 goes after the other particle: 주말에도 (on weekends too), 친구한테도 (to my friend too).
With a negative, 도 often means "not even": 물도 안 마셨어요 (I didn't even drink water). This adds a sense of surprise or emphasis.
도 itself has no politeness level, so it works in casual and polite speech alike. 나도 is casual "me too," 저도 is the polite version.

examples.en: I like coffee too.
My younger sibling came along too.
Do you work on weekends too?
I didn't even drink water.

compare.note: 만 means "only" and limits things, while 도 means "also" and adds things. 커피만 마셔요 is "I only drink coffee," 커피도 마셔요 is "I drink coffee too."
조차 also means "even," but it is stronger and mostly used for bad or disappointing situations. 도 is the everyday choice.

mistakes: Stacking 도 with 는 or 를, as in 저는도 or 커피를도. 도 replaces those particles: 저도, 커피도.

faq.q: What does 저도 mean?
faq.a: 저도 means "me too" or "I also" in polite speech. With friends you say 나도.

faq.q: Can 도 come after 에 or 에서?
faq.a: Yes. It goes after them: 집에도 (at home too), 회사에서도 (at the office too).

intro: 만 (man) means "only" or "just" and attaches right after a noun: 물만 means "only water." It limits what you are talking about to that one thing. You can use it with positive and negative verbs.
usage: 만 says "this and nothing else." 물만 마셨어요 means "I only drank water." It usually replaces 이/가 and 을/를.
With other particles like 에 or 한테, 만 comes after them: 주말에만 (only on weekends), 너한테만 (only to you).
만 also softens requests: 한 번만 (just once), 잠깐만요 (just a moment). This makes the request sound small and easy to say yes to.
만 has no politeness level of its own. The verb ending decides how polite the sentence is.

examples.en: I only drank water.
You're the only one I trust.
Please help me just this once.
I only exercise on weekends.

compare.note: 밖에 also means "only" but must be followed by a negative verb: 물밖에 안 마셨어요. 만 works with any verb: 물만 마셨어요.
도 adds ("also"), while 만 limits ("only").

mistakes: Putting 을/를 before 만, as in 물을만. The usual form is just 물만. In formal writing you may see 물만을, with 을 after 만.

faq.q: What is the difference between 만 and 밖에?
faq.a: Both mean "only," but 밖에 needs a negative verb after it (밖에 없어요), while 만 works with positive verbs (만 있어요). 밖에 often sounds like "not more than I wanted."

faq.q: What does 만 mean in 3년 만에?
faq.a: That is a different word written with a space. 3년 만에 means "for the first time in 3 years" or "after 3 years."

intro: 밖에 (bakke) means "only" or "nothing but," and it is always followed by a negative verb: 천 원밖에 없어요 means "I only have 1,000 won." Literally it says "outside of 1,000 won, there is nothing." It often carries a feeling that the amount is less than you would like.

formation.example: 세 시간 → 세 시간밖에 못 잤어요

usage: 밖에 looks like "only," but the sentence must end in a negative: 없다, 모르다, or a verb with 안 or 못. In English the verb is positive ("I only have"), but in Korean it is "I don't have anything except."
Compared with 만, 밖에 often sounds a little disappointed or apologetic: 이것밖에 없어요 can mean "this is all I have, sorry."
It also shows up in romantic or emotional lines like 너밖에 없어 ("you're all I have"). Politeness depends on the ending: 없어 is casual, 없어요 is polite.

examples.en: I only have 1,000 won.
I only got three hours of sleep.
You're the only one I have.
I only know a little Korean.

compare.note: 만 works with positive verbs (천 원만 있어요), while 밖에 needs a negative (천 원밖에 없어요). Both mean "only," but 밖에 stresses that it is not much.

mistakes: Using 밖에 with a positive verb, as in 천 원밖에 있어요. Say 천 원밖에 없어요 or 천 원만 있어요.

faq.q: Why does 밖에 need a negative verb?
faq.a: 밖 means "outside," so 밖에 literally means "outside of." 천 원밖에 없어요 is "outside of 1,000 won, there is nothing," which means you only have 1,000 won.

faq.q: What does 너밖에 없어 mean?
faq.a: It means "you're the only one" or "I have no one but you." It is casual and often used with close friends or partners.

intro: 한테 (hante) and 에게 (ege) mean "to" a person or animal, as in giving, telling or sending something to someone. 한테 is the everyday spoken form and 에게 sounds more written or formal. For places and things, Korean uses 에 instead.
usage: Use 한테 or 에게 with verbs like 주다 (give), 말하다 (tell), 전화하다 (call), 보내다 (send) and 묻다 (ask): 친구한테 전화했어요 (I called my friend).
한테 and 에게 mean the same thing. 한테 is relaxed and common in conversation; 에게 is common in writing, speeches and news. Neither one is rude.
When the person is someone you show respect to, like a grandparent or teacher, use 께 and an honorific verb: 할머니께 드렸어요 (I gave it to Grandma).
These only work with living things. For a place or an organization, use 에: 회사에 전화했어요 (I called the company).

examples.en: I called my friend.
I gave Mom a present.
Did you feed the puppy?
Who are you going to send it to?

compare.note: 에 is "to" for places and things (학교에 가요), while 한테/에게 is "to" for people and animals (친구한테 줘요).
한테서 means "from" a person (친구한테서 받았어요), while 한테 means "to" a person. In speech 서 is often dropped, so the verb tells you which one is meant.

mistakes: Using 한테 with a place, as in 학교한테 전화했어요. For places and organizations use 에: 학교에 전화했어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 한테 and 에게?
faq.a: They mean the same thing. 한테 is more casual and spoken, and 에게 is more common in writing or formal speech.

faq.q: When do I use 께 instead?
faq.a: Use 께 for people you show respect to, such as grandparents, teachers or customers, usually with an honorific verb like 드리다.

intro: 한테서 (hanteseo) and 에게서 (egeseo) mean "from" a person, as in getting, hearing or learning something from someone. 한테서 is the spoken form and 에게서 sounds more written. For places, Korean uses 에서 instead.
usage: Use 한테서 or 에게서 with verbs like 받다 (receive), 듣다 (hear), 배우다 (learn) and 빌리다 (borrow): 형한테서 배웠어요 (I learned it from my older brother).
In everyday speech, people often drop 서 and just say 한테: 친구한테 받았어요. The verb 받다 already makes it clear the thing came from the friend.
These are only for people and animals. For a place, use 에서: 학교에서 연락이 왔어요 (I got a message from the school).

examples.en: I got a text from a friend.
Who did you hear it from?
I borrowed clothes from my older sister.
I learned it from my older brother.

compare.note: 한테 and 에게 mean "to" a person, while 한테서 and 에게서 mean "from" a person.
에서 is "from" a place (회사에서 왔어요), while 한테서 is "from" a person.

mistakes: Using 한테서 with a place, as in 회사한테서 연락이 왔어요. For places use 에서: 회사에서 연락이 왔어요.

faq.q: Can I just say 한테 instead of 한테서?
faq.a: Often yes. With verbs like 받다, 듣다 and 배우다, people commonly drop 서 because the meaning is clear.

faq.q: Is 에게서 more polite than 한테서?
faq.a: Not more polite, just more formal and written. In conversation 한테서 or 한테 is normal at any politeness level.

intro: 보다 (boda) means "than" and attaches to the thing you are comparing against: 어제보다 추워요 means "it's colder than yesterday." It is often paired with 더 (more), but 더 is optional. As a particle, it is written attached to the noun.
usage: 보다 marks the thing being compared against, and the main topic usually takes 이/가 or 은/는: 형이 저보다 커요 (My brother is bigger than me).
더 (more) is often added for emphasis, but the comparison already works without it: 어제보다 추워요 and 어제보다 더 추워요 both mean "colder than yesterday."
생각보다 ("than I thought") is a very common chunk: 생각보다 쉬웠어요 (It was easier than I thought).
보다 has no politeness level. It also works in casual speech: 나보다 잘해 (You're better than me).

examples.en: I like tea more than coffee.
It's colder than yesterday.
My older brother is taller than me.
It was easier than I thought.

compare.note: 처럼 says two things are alike ("like"), while 보다 says one is more or less than the other ("than").
The verb 보다 means "to see" or, after -아/어, "to try." The particle 보다 attaches to a noun and means "than."

mistakes: Writing a space before the particle, as in 커피 보다. As a particle, 보다 is attached: 커피보다.

faq.q: Do I need 더 with 보다?
faq.a: No. 더 adds emphasis, but 보다 alone already makes a comparison.

faq.q: How do I say "better than" in Korean?
faq.a: Use 보다 with 낫다 (to be better): 이게 저것보다 나아요 (This is better than that).

intro: 처럼 (cheoreom) and 같이 (gachi) mean "like" or "as" and attach right after a noun: 아이처럼 웃어요 means "she laughs like a child." They describe how something is done or what it resembles. 처럼 is the more common of the two.
usage: 처럼 and 같이 compare how something is done or how it looks: 가수처럼 노래해요 (She sings like a singer). They usually mean the same thing in this use.
When 같이 is a particle it is attached to the noun (봄날같이). Be careful: 같이 on its own as an adverb means "together" (같이 가요, let's go together).
To describe a noun, use 같은 (from 같다) before it: 꿈 같은 이야기 (a dreamlike story). This 같은 is written with a space.
These particles have no politeness level of their own and work in casual or polite speech.

examples.en: She laughed like a child.
You sing as well as a singer.
It's warm like a spring day today.
Just do it like you usually do.

compare.note: 같이 as a separate word means "together": 친구랑 같이 가요. Only when attached to a noun does it mean "like."
보다 means "than" and shows a difference, while 처럼 shows that two things are alike.

mistakes: Writing 처럼 with a space, as in 아이 처럼. It is a particle, so it is attached: 아이처럼.

faq.q: What is the difference between 처럼 and 같이?
faq.a: As particles meaning "like," they are mostly interchangeable. 처럼 is more common and never confused with 같이 "together."

faq.q: How do I say "like me" in Korean?
faq.a: Say 나처럼 in casual speech or 저처럼 in polite speech.

intro: 마다 (mada) means "every" or "each" and attaches to a noun: 아침마다 means "every morning." It is often used for routines and repeated events. With people or things, it means each one is different or each one does something.

formation.example: 십 분 → 십 분마다, 이틀 → 이틀마다

usage: With time words, 마다 shows a routine: 주말마다 등산 가요 (I go hiking every weekend). It can replace a time particle like 에, so you say 아침마다, not 아침에마다.
With numbers it shows how often: 십 분마다 (every ten minutes), 이틀마다 (every two days).
With people or things, 마다 often means "each one is different": 사람마다 생각이 달라요 (Everyone thinks differently).
마다 has no politeness level and works in any speech style.

examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
I go hiking every weekend.
Everyone thinks differently.
The bus comes every ten minutes.

compare.note: 매 goes before a noun as a prefix (매일, 매주, 매년), while 마다 goes after it (날마다, 주마다). 매일 and 날마다 both mean "every day."

mistakes: Saying 매일마다. 매 and 마다 both mean "every," so 매일 or 날마다 alone is enough, even though you may hear 매일마다 in casual talk.

faq.q: What does 날마다 mean?
faq.a: 날마다 means "every day." It means the same as 매일.

faq.q: How do I say "every two days"?
faq.a: Use 이틀마다. For "every three hours," say 세 시간마다.

intro: (으)로 ((eu)ro) means "by," "with" or "toward": 지하철로 가요 means "I go by subway." It marks the tool or way you do something, the direction you move in, and your choice when ordering. Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ and 으로 after other consonants.
usage: Means or tool: 버스로 가요 (I go by bus), 손으로 먹어요 (I eat with my hands), 한국어로 말해요 (I speak in Korean).
Direction: 오른쪽으로 가세요 (Go to the right). Compared with 에, which marks the goal, (으)로 focuses on the direction you head in.
Choice: when ordering or deciding, (으)로 marks what you pick: 이걸로 할게요 (I'll go with this one).
(으)로 has no politeness level. The ㄹ rule is the main thing to remember: 지하철로, not 지하철으로.

examples.en: I go by subway.
You can eat it with your hands.
Please go to the right.
I'll have an iced americano.

compare.note: 에 marks the destination (학교에 가요, I go to school), while (으)로 marks the direction or route (학교 쪽으로 가요, I head toward the school). With places, both are often possible.
에서 marks where an action happens or "from" a place. (으)로 marks the way or direction.

mistakes: Using 으로 after ㄹ, as in 지하철으로 or 연필으로. Nouns ending in ㄹ take 로: 지하철로, 연필로.

faq.q: When do I use 으로 and when do I use 로?
faq.a: Use 로 after a vowel or ㄹ (버스로, 지하철로) and 으로 after any other consonant (손으로).

faq.q: What does 이걸로 할게요 mean?
faq.a: It means "I'll take this one." (으)로 marks your choice, and you hear it a lot when ordering.

intro: 의 (ui) means "'s" or "of" and shows that something belongs to someone: 친구의 생일 means "my friend's birthday." In speech, 의 is often pronounced like 에, and it is frequently left out. With 저, 나 and 너 it shortens to 제, 내 and 네.
usage: 의 links two nouns: the owner first, then the thing: 친구의 생일 (my friend's birthday), 한국의 겨울 (Korea's winter).
In everyday speech, 의 is often dropped when the meaning is clear: 친구 생일, 엄마 가방. Keeping it can sound a bit formal or written.
With pronouns, use the short forms: 제 (my, polite), 내 (my, casual), 네 (your, casual). Many people say 니 for 네 in speech so it doesn't sound like 내.
When 의 means "of," it is often pronounced [에], which is accepted standard pronunciation.

examples.en: It's my friend's birthday.
Winters in Korea are cold.
My name is Minji.
What is the title of this song?

compare.note: These are shortened forms of 저의, 나의 and 너의. In conversation, the short forms are what people actually say.

mistakes: Saying 나의 or 저의 in everyday speech. It sounds stiff or poetic; use 내 or 제 instead: 제 이름은...
Pronouncing every 의 as [의]. As the possessive particle it is usually said [에]: 친구의 sounds like 친구에.

faq.q: How do you pronounce 의 in 친구의?
faq.a: As the possessive particle, 의 is usually pronounced [에], so 친구의 sounds like 친구에.

faq.q: Can I leave out 의?
faq.a: Yes, very often. 친구 집 and 엄마 가방 are completely natural in speech.

intro: (이)나 ((i)na) means "or" between two nouns: 커피나 차 means "coffee or tea." It can also mean "or something" to soften a suggestion, and after a number it means "as many as" to show surprise. Use 나 after a vowel and 이나 after a consonant.
usage: Between nouns, (이)나 means "or": 커피나 차 (coffee or tea). For verbs and adjectives, use -거나 instead.
In suggestions, (이)나 means "or something" and makes the idea sound casual: 영화나 볼까요? (Shall we watch a movie or something?).
After a number, (이)나 means "as many as" or "a whole," showing the amount feels large: 두 시간이나 기다렸어요 (I waited a whole two hours).
(이)나 has no politeness level. Note that 나 here is not the word 나 meaning "I."

examples.en: Would you like coffee or tea?
Shall we watch a movie or something this weekend?
I waited a whole two hours.
Do you have bread or snacks?

compare.note: -거나 joins verbs and adjectives (먹거나 자요), while (이)나 joins nouns (빵이나 밥).
하고 and (이)랑 mean "and" (both things), while (이)나 means "or" (one of them).

mistakes: Using (이)나 between verbs, as in 먹나 자요. For verbs, use -거나: 먹거나 자요.

faq.q: When do I use 이나 and when do I use 나?
faq.a: Use 나 after a vowel (커피나) and 이나 after a consonant (빵이나).

faq.q: What does 두 시간이나 mean?
faq.a: It means "as long as two hours" or "a whole two hours." (이)나 after a number shows the amount feels like a lot.

intro: 아/야 (a/ya) is added to a name when you call someone, like "Hey, Jisu!": 지수야 or 민준아. It is friendly and casual, used with friends, younger people, children and pets. Use 야 after a vowel and 아 after a consonant.
usage: 아/야 goes on a given name when you are calling or talking directly to someone: 지수야, 밥 먹었어? (Jisu, did you eat?). It sounds close and warm.
Only use it with people you can speak casually to: friends your age, younger siblings, children, or pets. Never use it with teachers, bosses, older people or strangers.
In casual sentences, consonant-ending names often get an extra 이 when they are not being called: 민준이가 왔어 (Minjun came). That 이 is different from the calling 아.
