On its own, 야! means "hey!" It is fine with close friends but rude to strangers or older people.

examples.en: Jisu, did you eat?
Minjun, get up!
Subin, thank you.
Nabi, come here.

compare.note: 씨 after a name (지수 씨) is polite and used with adults you are not close to. 아/야 is only for close, casual relationships.

mistakes: Using 아/야 with someone older or senior, like a teacher or boss. Use a title instead, such as 선생님 or 팀장님.
Mixing up the forms, as in 지수아 or 민준야. Vowel-ending names take 야, consonant-ending names take 아.

faq.q: Why do some names get 아 and others get 야?
faq.a: It depends on the last sound. Names ending in a vowel take 야 (지수야) and names ending in a consonant take 아 (민준아).

faq.q: Can I use 아/야 with a full name?
faq.a: Usually not. With a full name, Koreans tend to say just the name, like 김민준!, which can sound serious, as if someone is in trouble.

intro: 조차 (jocha) and 마저 (majeo) mean "even" and attach to a noun: 이름조차 몰라요 means "I don't even know their name." They are used for the most basic or last thing you would expect, usually in a negative or disappointing situation. They are stronger than 도.
usage: 조차 means "not even the most basic thing": 물조차 못 마셨어요 (I couldn't even drink water). It is mostly used with negatives or bad news.
마저 means "even this last one too," often when things keep getting worse: 너마저 그렇게 생각해? (Even you think that way?).
Both sound more emphatic than 도 and are common in writing, news and emotional speech. In relaxed conversation, 도 is often used for the same idea.

examples.en: I don't even know their name.
I couldn't even drink water.

examples.context: Feeling let down by a friend
examples.en: Even you think that way?
It's raining, and on top of that the wind is blowing.

compare.note: 도 can also mean "even" (물도 안 마셨어요), but it is lighter and more everyday. 조차 and 마저 sound stronger.
까지 can mean "even" in good or bad situations (선물까지 줬어요, he even gave me a gift). 조차 and 마저 lean toward unwelcome situations.

mistakes: Using 조차 for something pleasant, as in 선물조차 줬어요. For a nice surprise, use 까지: 선물까지 줬어요.

faq.q: What is the difference between 조차 and 마저?
faq.a: 조차 points to the most basic thing that did not happen. 마저 points to the last remaining thing being affected too. They often overlap, and both are mostly negative.

faq.q: Is 조차 formal?
faq.a: It sounds a bit strong and is common in writing, but it is fine in speech when you want emphasis.

intro: -들 (-deul) makes a noun plural, a bit like English "-s": 친구들 means "friends." Unlike English, it is often optional, and Koreans leave it out when the plural is already clear. It is used most with people.
usage: -들 marks more than one, especially with people: 학생들 (students), 아이들 (children). With things, it is less common: people often just say 책 for "books."
When a number or a word like 많이 already shows there are several, -들 is usually not needed: 사과 세 개 (three apples).
Particles come after -들: 친구들이, 친구들하고, 친구들한테.
In casual speech, 들 can also attach to other words to show the action is done by several people: 많이들 드세요 (Everyone, please eat a lot).

examples.en: I hung out with my friends.
There are a lot of students.
The children are laughing.
Everyone, please eat a lot.

compare.note: 여러분 means "everyone" or "you all" when addressing a group. It is already plural, so it does not need 들.

mistakes: Adding 들 to every plural thing, as in 사과들 세 개. When a number shows the amount, just say 사과 세 개.

faq.q: Do I always need 들 for plurals in Korean?
faq.a: No. -들 is optional and often left out, especially for things or when the context makes the plural clear.

faq.q: What does 많이들 mean?
faq.a: It means "a lot" with the idea that everyone in the group is doing it, as in 많이들 드세요 (everyone, eat up).

intro: -적 (-jeok) works like English "-ic" or "-al": it turns a Sino-Korean noun into a describing word, as in 개인 (individual) → 개인적 (personal). It is usually followed by 인 before a noun, 으로 as an adverb, or 이다 at the end of a sentence. You will see it everywhere in news, essays and everyday opinions.

formation.when: At the end of a sentence

usage: -적 changes a noun into an idea of "having that quality": 역사 (history) → 역사적 (historic), 경제 (economy) → 경제적 (economic).
It almost never stands alone in speech. Add 인 before a noun (역사적인 날), 으로 to make an adverb (개인적으로, personally), or 이다 to end the sentence (현실적이에요).
-적 only works with certain Sino-Korean (Chinese-origin) nouns, so it is best to learn each word as a set. 개인적으로 (personally) is one of the most useful.

examples.en: Personally, I like this one.
I have a basic question.
That's very realistic.
It's a historic day.

compare.note: -스럽다 makes adjectives that describe a feeling or impression (자연스럽다, natural). -적 is more abstract and formal, closer to English "-ic" or "-al."

mistakes: Adding -적 to native Korean words or to any noun at all. It only goes with set Sino-Korean nouns, so learn words like 개인적, 기본적 and 현실적 one by one.

faq.q: What does 개인적으로 mean?
faq.a: 개인적으로 means "personally" or "in my opinion." It is a common way to start an opinion.

faq.q: Is -적 the same 적 as in -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다?
faq.a: No. In -(으)ㄴ 적이 있다, 적 is a separate word meaning "a time" or "an experience." The -적 on this page is a suffix like "-ic."

intro: -답다 (-dapda) means "worthy of" or "just like a true" something: 프로답다 means "like a real pro." You attach it to a noun to say someone or something lives up to what it is. It follows the ㅂ-irregular pattern, so 답다 becomes 다워요.
usage: -답다 says something matches the ideal of what it is: 어른답게 행동하세요 (Act like a grown-up should). It is usually positive.
With a person's name or 너, it means "that's so you": 역시 너다워 (Classic you).
Because it is ㅂ-irregular, the ㅂ turns into 우 before vowels: 다워요, 다운, 다웠어요. Before consonants it stays: 답게, 답지 않아요.
Politeness comes from the ending: 너다워 is casual, 너다워요 is polite.

examples.en: That's so you.
He finished it like a true pro.
Please act like a grown-up.
It's real fall weather.

compare.note: 남자 같아요 means "he (or she) looks like a man" (resemblance). 남자다워요 means "he is manly, as a man should be" (living up to it).
어른스럽다 means a child acts mature, like an adult. 어른답다 means an adult acts the way an adult should.

mistakes: Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular change, as in 너답어요. The correct form is 너다워요.

faq.q: What does 너답다 mean?
faq.a: 너답다 means "that's so you" or "typical of you," usually said with warmth or a little teasing.

faq.q: What is the difference between -답다 and 같다?
faq.a: 같다 is about resembling something, while -답다 is about living up to what something should be.

intro: -스럽다 (-seureopda) means "-ish" or "-ful": it turns a noun into an adjective meaning "having that feeling or quality," as in 사랑 (love) → 사랑스럽다 (lovely). Many common adjectives are made this way, like 자연스럽다 (natural). It follows the ㅂ-irregular pattern, so it becomes 스러워요.
usage: -스럽다 describes the feeling or impression something gives: 사랑스러워요 (lovely), 걱정스러워요 (worrying), 촌스러워요 (tacky, countrified).
It does not mean the thing actually is that noun. 어른스럽다 is used for a child who seems mature, not for an adult.
Because it is ㅂ-irregular, 스럽 becomes 스러우 before vowels: 스러워요, 스러운, 스러웠어요. Before consonants it stays: 스럽게, 스럽지 않아요.
You cannot add it to just any noun. Treat words like 자연스럽다 and 사랑스럽다 as vocabulary to learn.

examples.en: Your pronunciation sounds natural.
The puppy is so lovely.
This outfit is a bit tacky.
What a fancy restaurant.

compare.note: -답다 means living up to what you are (어른답다, an adult acting properly). -스럽다 means giving that impression (어른스럽다, a child acting grown-up).
-적 is more formal and abstract ("-ic, -al"), while -스럽다 makes everyday feeling adjectives.

mistakes: Forgetting the ㅂ-irregular change, as in 자연스럽어요. The correct form is 자연스러워요.

faq.q: What does 자연스럽다 mean?
faq.a: 자연스럽다 means "natural," as in sounding or looking natural. It is one of the most common -스럽다 words.

faq.q: Can I add -스럽다 to any noun?
faq.a: No. Only certain nouns take it, so it is best to learn each word on its own.

intro: -겠어요 (-gesseoyo) and -(으)ㄹ 거예요 (-(eu)l geoyeyo) can both mean "will," but they are not the same. -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is the everyday future for plans and general guesses, while -겠어요 shows a decision made right now or a guess based on what you see. Knowing which to pick makes your Korean sound much more natural.

formation.when: -(으)ㄹ 거예요: stem ending in a vowel
-(으)ㄹ 거예요: stem ending in a consonant

usage: -(으)ㄹ 거예요 is the default future: plans you already have (내일 친구를 만날 거예요) and general guesses (아마 집에 있을 거예요, he's probably home). It works for anyone: I, you, he or she.

-겠어요 shows the speaker's will at this moment ("I will, I promise") or an instant guess from what you see or hear: 맛있겠어요! (That looks delicious!). For intention, it is used for yourself, not for other people's plans.

-겠- also appears in fixed polite phrases: 알겠습니다 (I understand), 잘 먹겠습니다 (thanks for the meal), 처음 뵙겠습니다 (nice to meet you). In the formal -겠습니다 form it sounds firm and respectful, as in promises to a boss.

examples.en: I'm going to meet a friend tomorrow.
Wow, that looks delicious!
From now on, I will come early.
He's probably at home.

compare.note: -(으)ㄹ게요 is a promise or decision made with the listener in mind (제가 할게요, I'll do it for you). -겠어요 sounds more formal and firm.
-(으)려고 해요 means "I'm planning to" or "I intend to," close to -(으)ㄹ 거예요 for plans but with more focus on intention.

mistakes: Using -겠어요 for someone else's plans, as in 민수 씨가 내일 가겠어요. That sounds like a guess. To state their plan, say 민수 씨가 내일 갈 거예요.
Saying 맛있을 거예요 when looking at food in front of you. That sounds like a general prediction; 맛있겠어요 is the natural reaction.

faq.q: Which one should I use for future plans?
faq.a: Use -(으)ㄹ 거예요. It is the natural choice for plans and schedules, for yourself and for other people.

faq.q: Is -겠- always about the future?
faq.a: No. It can also be a guess about now or the past: 힘들었겠어요 means "that must have been hard."

intro: -던 (-deon) describes a noun with a past action that was ongoing, repeated or unfinished, like "that I used to" or "that I was": 자주 가던 카페 means "the cafe I used to go to often." It looks back at the past with a feeling of memory. Compare 먹은 빵 (the bread I ate) with 먹던 빵 (the bread I was eating).

formation.example: 가다 → 가던 카페, 먹다 → 먹던 빵
가다 → 갔던 식당, 먹다 → 먹었던 음식

usage: -던 attaches to a verb to describe a noun with something from the past that was not finished or happened again and again: 하던 일 (the work I was doing), 살던 동네 (the neighborhood I used to live in).
-았/었던 is for a past event that was completed, often just once: 작년에 갔던 식당 (the restaurant I went to last year). In everyday speech the two often overlap.
-(으)ㄴ is the simple finished past: 먹은 빵 is bread that was eaten, while 먹던 빵 is bread someone was in the middle of eating.
-던 itself has no politeness level, because it only describes a noun. The ending at the end of the sentence decides how polite you are.

examples.en: Where did the coffee I was drinking go?
The cafe I used to go to often is gone.
This is the neighborhood I lived in as a kid.
Please go on with what you were doing.

compare.note: -(으)ㄴ marks a finished past action (먹은 빵, bread that was eaten). -던 marks one that was ongoing or unfinished (먹던 빵, bread someone was eating).
-곤 하다 ends a sentence to say "I used to often do" (자주 가곤 했어요), while -던 describes a noun (자주 가던 곳).

mistakes: Using 먹은 when you mean something is left unfinished. 먹던 빵 is the half-eaten bread; 먹은 빵 is bread that was eaten.

faq.q: What is the difference between -던 and -았/었던?
faq.a: -던 suggests something ongoing, repeated or unfinished. -았/었던 suggests something completed in the past, often once. In casual speech they are often used for the same idea.

faq.q: Does -던 mean "used to"?
faq.a: Often, yes. 가던 카페 is "the cafe I used to go to." But it can also mean "was doing," as in 하던 일 (the work I was doing).
